name: Paint Calculator
h1: Paint Calculator: How Much Interior Paint Do I Need?
intro: Calculate exact gallons and quarts of wall, ceiling, and primer paint for any room size with automatic door and window deductions.
metaTitle: Paint Calculator: How Much Paint Do I Need? | BuildMath
metaDescription: Free interior paint calculator. Enter room dimensions, doors, windows, and coats to get exact gallons, quarts, primer, and material cost estimates.

inputs.name: doors
inputs.label: Number of Doors
inputs.tooltip: Deducts 21 sq ft per standard 3×7 ft interior door.

inputs.name: windows
inputs.label: Number of Windows
inputs.tooltip: Deducts 15 sq ft per standard 3×5 ft residential window.

inputs.name: coveragePerGallon
inputs.label: Paint Coverage Rate
inputs.tooltip: Manufacturer standard (Sherwin-Williams / Behr / Benjamin Moore) is 350–400 sq ft/gal on smooth drywall; drop to 250–300 sq ft/gal for heavy knockdown texture.

inputs.name: primerCoveragePerGallon
inputs.label: Primer Coverage Rate
inputs.tooltip: PVA and stain-blocking primers cover 200–300 sq ft/gal on bare drywall or patched plaster.

inputs.name: wastePercent
inputs.label: Waste & Roller Absorption
inputs.tooltip: Accounts for paint left in roller nap, tray liner, and touch-up reserve (5% standard).

inputs.name: pricePerGallon
inputs.label: Paint Price per Gallon
inputs.tooltip: US mid-grade 100% acrylic latex interior paint average ($32–$68/gal).

inputs.name: primerPricePerGallon
inputs.label: Primer Price per Gallon
inputs.tooltip: US retail multi-surface interior primer average ($21–$38/gal).

quickReferenceMeta.title: Gallons of Paint for Common Room Sizes (2 Coats, No Ceiling)

howToCalculate.formula: Gallons = [ (2 × (Length + Width) × Height − (Doors × 21) − (Windows × 15) + Ceiling) × Coats ÷ 350 ] × (1 + Waste%)
steps: Add the length and width of the room and multiply by 2 to find the total wall perimeter in linear feet.
Multiply the perimeter by the ceiling height to get the gross wall area in square feet.
Subtract 21 sq ft for every standard door (3 ft × 7 ft) and 15 sq ft for every standard window (3 ft × 5 ft).
If painting the ceiling the same color, add Length × Width to your net wall area.
Multiply the net area by the number of coats (usually 2) and divide by 350 sq ft per gallon.

workedExample.title: Painting a 12×12 ft Bedroom with 8-ft Ceilings
workedExample.scenario: You are painting a 12 ft × 12 ft bedroom with 8-ft walls, 2 doors (entry + closet), and 2 windows using 2 coats of eggshell wall paint.
steps: Perimeter = 2 × (12 + 12) = 48 linear feet.
Gross Wall Area = 48 ft × 8 ft = 384 sq ft.
Openings = (2 doors × 21 sq ft) + (2 windows × 15 sq ft) = 72 sq ft.
Net Wall Area = 384 − 72 = 312 sq ft.
Paint for 2 Coats (with 5% roller waste) = (312 × 2 ÷ 350) × 1.05 = 1.87 gallons.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Round up to 2 gallons of wall paint (or 1 gallon + 4 quarts).

tipsAndMistakes: Box your paint cans: if your project requires 2 or more gallons of the same color, pour them together into a clean 5-gallon bucket ("boxing") so slight tint variations between cans never show on the wall.
Buy 5-gallon buckets for whole-house jobs: a 5-gallon pail usually costs 15%–20% less than five individual 1-gallon cans.
Use PVA primer on fresh drywall mud: bare joint compound soaks up topcoat binder and leaves dull "flashing" patches unless sealed with dedicated drywall primer first.
Match roller nap thickness to wall texture: use a 3/8-inch microfiber nap for smooth or light orange-peel walls, and a 1/2-inch or 3/4-inch nap for heavy knockdown plaster.
Don’t stretch paint thin: trying to squeeze 450+ sq ft out of a single gallon leaves pinholes and roller tracks that require a third coat anyway.
Pull painter’s tape while the final coat is still slightly wet: scoring dried latex over tape can peel the fresh edge right off the trim.

faqs.question: How many square feet does 1 gallon of interior paint cover?
faqs.answer: One gallon of quality interior acrylic latex paint covers 350 to 400 square feet in a single coat on smooth, primed drywall. On porous bare drywall, acoustic ceilings, or heavy knockdown texture, coverage drops to 250–300 square feet per gallon.

faqs.question: Do I really need two coats if I buy "paint and primer in one"?
faqs.answer: Yes in most cases. Self-priming paint has higher solids for better hide, but rolling a single coat by hand inevitably leaves microscopic holiday thin spots and roller lap marks. Two coats ensure uniform sheen, true color depth, and scrubbability.

faqs.question: Should I use a tinted primer when painting over dark walls?
faqs.answer: If you are painting a light color over navy, charcoal, burgundy, or bright red, ask the paint desk to tint your high-hide primer to 50% of your finish color (or medium gray). One coat of tinted primer plus two topcoats prevents bleed-through.

faqs.question: How much paint do I need for baseboards and door trim?
faqs.answer: One quart of semi-gloss or urethane alkyd trim enamel covers roughly 85 to 100 linear feet of standard 3.25-inch baseboard (two coats), or about 3 to 4 standard six-panel interior doors on both sides.

faqs.question: How long does leftover interior latex paint last in the can?
faqs.answer: Unopened latex paint lasts up to 10 years if stored between 50°F and 80°F without freezing. Opened cans last 2 to 5 years if you wipe the rim clean, lay plastic wrap over the opening, and tap the lid shut with a rubber mallet.

name: Exterior Paint Calculator
h1: Exterior Paint Calculator: How Much House Paint Do I Need?
intro: Estimate 1-gallon cans and 5-gallon buckets of exterior siding and trim paint using your house perimeter, story height, gables, and openings.
metaTitle: Exterior House Paint Calculator (Siding & Trim) | BuildMath
metaDescription: Calculate how many gallons of exterior paint your house needs. Includes gable triangles, rough stucco/wood coverage rates, and trim enamel estimates.

inputs.name: wallHeight
inputs.label: Exterior Wall Height (Eave Line)
inputs.tooltip: Typically 9–10 ft for 1-story homes and 18–20 ft for 2-story homes.

inputs.name: coveragePerGallon
inputs.label: Siding Coverage Rate
inputs.tooltip: Smooth Hardie/wood lap siding averages 300 sq ft/gal; rough cedar shakes or unpainted stucco average 150–225 sq ft/gal.

inputs.name: wastePercent
inputs.label: Sprayer / Wind Overspray Waste
inputs.tooltip: Use 5–10% for brush & roller; use 15–20% for airless sprayer overspray.

inputs.name: pricePerGallon
inputs.label: Exterior Paint Price per Gallon
inputs.tooltip: US retail 100% acrylic exterior house paint average ($42–$79/gal).

quickReferenceMeta.title: Exterior Paint Gallons by Home Size (2 Coats + 10% Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Gallons = [ ((Perimeter × Wall Height) + (Gables × 0.5 × Width × Height) − Openings) × Coats ÷ Coverage ] × (1 + Waste%)
steps: Walk the outside of your house and add all four wall lengths together to get the House Perimeter.
Multiply the perimeter by the height from the foundation sill to the roof soffit eave.
For each triangular roof gable, multiply 0.5 × Gable Width × Gable Peak Height and add to the wall area.
Subtract 21 sq ft per entry door, 15 sq ft per window, and 112 sq ft per 2-car garage door.
Multiply by the number of coats, divide by your siding coverage rate (300 sq ft/gal default), and add 10% waste.

workedExample.title: 1,600 sq ft Ranch Home Repaint
workedExample.scenario: A single-story home has a 160-ft perimeter, 10-ft walls, 2 gables (24 ft wide × 6 ft high), 2 doors, 10 windows, and 1 garage door.
steps: Main Wall Area = 160 × 10 = 1,600 sq ft.
Gables = 2 × (0.5 × 24 × 6) = 144 sq ft. Gross Area = 1,744 sq ft.
Openings = (2 × 21) + (10 × 15) + 112 = 304 sq ft. Net Area = 1,440 sq ft.
2 Coats @ 300 sq ft/gal = 2,880 ÷ 300 = 9.60 gallons.
With 10% waste = 9.60 × 1.10 = 10.56 gallons.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 11 gallons of siding paint (two 5-gallon buckets + one 1-gallon can) plus 2 gallons of trim paint.

tipsAndMistakes: Back-roll when spraying: if you apply exterior paint with an airless sprayer, have a helper immediately roll over the wet paint with a 1/2" nap roller to push paint into siding pores and cracks.
Check overnight low temperatures: standard acrylic exterior paint fails to coalesce if surface temperatures drop below 35°F–50°F within 24 hours of painting.
Never paint vinyl siding darker than its original shade unless you use "Vinyl-Safe" solar-reflective pigments—dark regular paint absorbs heat and warps vinyl panels.
Wait 48–72 hours after pressure washing: painting over damp wood siding traps moisture that blisters the new film in the first summer sun.
Use elastomeric masonry caulk around windows and butt joints before priming.
Spot-prime bare cedar or redwood knots with oil-based or shellac stain-blocking primer to stop tannin bleed.

faqs.question: How much paint does a 2,000 sq ft house need on the exterior?
faqs.answer: A typical 2,000 sq ft home has roughly 1,800 to 2,200 square feet of net exterior siding area. For two full coats of 100% acrylic paint at 300 sq ft per gallon, expect to need 13 to 16 gallons for the siding plus 2 to 3 gallons for trim, fascia, and soffits.

faqs.question: How much does rough stucco or brick reduce paint coverage?
faqs.answer: Porous unpainted stucco, cinder block, or rough-sawn cedar shakes absorb heavily on the first coat, averaging only 150 to 200 sq ft per gallon. Set the Coverage Rate field in the calculator to 200 sq ft/gal for rough masonry.

faqs.question: Is flat, satin, or semi-gloss better for exterior siding?
faqs.answer: Satin (or low-luster eggshell) is the preferred sheen for lap siding because it sheds dirt and rainwater while hiding minor wood grain imperfections. Reserve semi-gloss for fascia, window trim, shutters, and front doors.

faqs.question: How much paint does an airless sprayer waste compared to rolling?
faqs.answer: Airless sprayers atomize paint under high pressure, losing 15% to 25% of the paint to wind drift and masking paper overspray. Increase the Waste slider to 15% or 20% if spraying.

faqs.question: How often does a house exterior need repainting?
faqs.answer: High-grade 100% acrylic latex over fiber-cement or aluminum lasts 10 to 15 years. Wood siding typically requires recoating every 5 to 8 years depending on sun exposure, while painted stucco lasts 8 to 12 years.

name: Deck Stain Calculator
h1: Deck Stain Calculator: How Much Deck Stain & Sealer Do I Need?
intro: Calculate gallons of deck stain for floorboards, two-sided railings, spindles, and stairs with separate 1st-coat and 2nd-coat absorption rates.
metaTitle: Deck Stain Calculator (Floor, Railings & Stairs) | BuildMath
metaDescription: Estimate gallons of deck stain and sealer for wood decks. Accounts for floorboards, both sides of railings, stair steps, and dry-wood absorption.

inputs.name: railingHeight
inputs.label: Railing Height
inputs.tooltip: IRC code requires 36" (3 ft) minimum guardrail height on residential decks.

inputs.name: firstCoatCoverage
inputs.label: 1st Coat Coverage Rate
inputs.tooltip: Dry, weathered pressure-treated pine or cedar absorbs 1st coat at ~150–225 sq ft/gal.

inputs.name: secondCoatCoverage
inputs.label: 2nd Coat Coverage Rate
inputs.tooltip: Once wood pores are saturated by the 1st coat, the 2nd coat spreads ~300 sq ft/gal.

inputs.name: wastePercent
inputs.label: Gap Drip & Applicator Waste
inputs.tooltip: Accounts for stain dripping between 1/8" deck board gaps (5% with pad, 15% if sprayed).

inputs.name: pricePerGallon
inputs.label: Deck Stain Price per Gallon
inputs.tooltip: US retail penetrating semi-transparent or solid deck stain average ($36–$65/gal).

quickReferenceMeta.title: Gallons of Deck Stain by Deck Size (Includes Railings & Stairs, 2 Coats)

howToCalculate.formula: Total Area = (Deck L × W) + (Railing Length × Height × 2) + (Steps × Width × 1.5); Gallons = (Area ÷ 200) + (Area ÷ 300)
steps: Multiply Deck Length × Deck Width to find the flat floorboard area.
Multiply Railing Linear Feet × Railing Height × 2 (because spindles and rails must be stained on both inside and outside faces).
Multiply the number of steps by Stair Width × 1.5 ft (10" tread + 7.5" riser) to get the stair surface area.
Add Deck + Railings + Stairs to get Total Stainable Square Footage.
Divide by 200 sq ft/gal for the first coat and 300 sq ft/gal for the second coat, then add 5% waste.

workedExample.title: Staining a 12×16 ft Deck with 28 ft of Railing & 4 Steps
workedExample.scenario: You have a 12×16 ft pressure-treated deck, 28 linear feet of 3-ft-tall wood railing, and 4 steps (4 ft wide), applying 2 coats.
steps: Floor Area = 16 × 12 = 192 sq ft.
Railing Area (2 sides) = 28 ft × 3 ft × 2 = 168 sq ft.
Stair Area = 4 steps × 4 ft × 1.5 ft = 24 sq ft. Total Area = 384 sq ft.
1st Coat @ 200 sq ft/gal = 1.92 gal; 2nd Coat @ 300 sq ft/gal = 1.28 gal.
Total with 5% waste = (1.92 + 1.28) × 1.05 = 3.36 gallons.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Buy 4 gallons of deck stain (or one 5-gallon pail for extra touch-up).

tipsAndMistakes: Railings nearly double your square footage: forgetting to count both sides of wood balusters is the #1 reason homeowners run out of deck stain halfway through.

Let new pressure-treated lumber dry first: fresh green-treated pine is saturated with waterborne preservatives; wait 3 to 6 months until water droplets soak in immediately (the "splash test") before staining.
Stain 2–3 boards end-to-end at a time: rolling across all boards perpendicular to the grain leaves dark overlapping "lap marks" where wet stain meets dry stain.
Use an oxygen-bleach deck cleaner + wood brightener (oxalic acid) rather than chlorine bleach, which breaks down wood lignin fibers.
Do not apply film-forming solid stain over oil-based penetrating stain without stripping first—it will peel after the first winter snow.
Stain railings and spindles first, then work your way off the deck floorboards toward the stairs so you never step in wet stain.

faqs.question: Why does the first coat of deck stain use more gallons than the second coat?
faqs.answer: Dry, sun-weathered exterior decking acts like a sponge on the first pass, absorbing stain deep into the wood grain at roughly 150 to 200 sq ft per gallon. The second coat sits on already-saturated wood fibers and spreads 250 to 350 sq ft per gallon.

faqs.question: Should I use semi-transparent or solid deck stain?
faqs.answer: Use penetrating semi-transparent oil or hybrid stain on newer decks in good condition—it highlights the natural wood grain and fades gradually without peeling. Reserve solid-color acrylic deck stain for older, heavily weathered decks with mismatched replacement boards.

faqs.question: Can I apply two coats of penetrating oil stain after the first coat dries?
faqs.answer: No! Most penetrating oil stains require "wet-on-wet" application (applying the second coat within 15–30 minutes while the first coat is still damp). If the first coat cures completely, it seals the pores and the second coat will remain sticky on top.

faqs.question: How long after rain can I stain my deck?
faqs.answer: Wait at least 48 hours of dry, sunny weather (below 15% wood moisture content on a pin moisture meter). Staining damp wood locks moisture inside and causes premature blistering and mildew.

faqs.question: What is the fastest tool to stain deck boards and spindles?
faqs.answer: Use a 7-inch deck stain pad with a gap brush attachment on an extension pole for the floorboards, and a painter’s mitt or 4-inch mini microfiber roller plus a 2.5-inch brush for spindles.

name: Wallpaper Calculator
h1: Wallpaper Calculator: How Many Rolls of Wallpaper Do I Need?
intro: Calculate single and double rolls of wallpaper with usable coverage deductions and pattern-repeat matching waste.
metaTitle: Wallpaper Roll Calculator (Single & Double) | BuildMath
metaDescription: Calculate how many double rolls of wallpaper you need. Includes usable roll coverage (25 sq ft/single), pattern repeat waste, and door/window deductions.

inputs.name: usableSingleRollCoverage
inputs.label: Usable Coverage per Single Roll
inputs.tooltip: A standard US single roll is ~28–30 sq ft gross, yielding 25 sq ft of usable wall coverage after top/bottom trim.

inputs.name: wastePercent
inputs.label: Top/Bottom Trim & Cut Waste
inputs.tooltip: Standard 10% allowance for ceiling/baseboard trimming and corner wraps.

inputs.name: pricePerDoubleRoll
inputs.label: Price per Double Roll
inputs.tooltip: Wallpaper is priced by the single roll but packaged and sold in 2-roll "double roll" bolts ($34–$95 avg).

quickReferenceMeta.title: Wallpaper Rolls Needed for Common Rooms (Includes 10% Repeat + 10% Cut Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Single Rolls = [ ((Wall Perimeter × Height) − Openings) ÷ 25 ] × (1 + Pattern Repeat% + Cut Waste%); Double Rolls = ceil(Single Rolls ÷ 2)
steps: Multiply your total wall width (or room perimeter) by the ceiling height to get gross wall square footage.
Subtract 21 sq ft per door and 15 sq ft per window.
Divide the net wall area by 25 sq ft (the usable coverage of a standard single roll).
Add your pattern-repeat waste (0% random, 10% straight match, 20% drop match) plus 10% trimming waste.
Divide single rolls by 2 and round UP to get Double Rolls (since wallpaper is sold in double-roll bolts).

workedExample.title: Wallpapering a 12×12 ft Dining Room (48 ft Perimeter)
workedExample.scenario: You are hanging straight-match wallpaper (10% repeat waste) in a room with a 48-ft perimeter, 8-ft ceilings, 2 doors, and 2 windows.
steps: Gross Wall Area = 48 × 8 = 384 sq ft.
Base Single Rolls = 312 ÷ 25 = 12.48 single rolls.
With 10% repeat + 10% trim waste (20% total) = 12.48 × 1.20 = 14.98 single rolls.
Double Rolls = 14.98 ÷ 2 = 7.49 → Round up to 8 double rolls.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 8 double rolls (16 single rolls equivalent).

tipsAndMistakes: Understand Single vs. Double Rolls: stores almost always advertise the price per "single roll" for comparison, but only ship continuous "double roll" bolts (50 sq ft usable) so you can cut three full 8-ft vertical drops per bolt instead of just one.
Check dye lot / batch numbers on every roll before cutting: never mix two different production run numbers on the same wall.

Always prime painted drywall with pigmented acrylic wallpaper primer/sealer (like ROMAN PRO-977) first—never hang wallpaper over regular flat latex paint, or the drywall paper will tear when you remove it years later.
Plumb your first strip with a 4-foot level or laser line: house corners are almost never plumb, so aligning your first strip to a crooked corner will tilt the entire pattern across the wall.
Order 1 extra double roll at checkout: popular patterns go out of stock or change dye lots within months.
Change your snap-off razor blade every 3 to 4 cuts along the baseboard so wet paper never tears.

faqs.question: Why is usable wallpaper coverage 25 sq ft when the roll says 28 or 30 sq ft?
faqs.answer: A standard American single roll measures 20.5 inches wide by 16.5 feet long (28.18 sq ft), and a Euro roll is 20.8 inches by 16.5 feet (28.6 sq ft). However, you must leave 2 inches of extra overhang at the ceiling and 2 inches at the baseboard on every vertical drop, leaving ~25 sq ft of usable area.

faqs.question: Why should I buy double rolls instead of single rolls?
faqs.answer: A single roll is only 16.5 feet long. On an 8-foot wall, cutting one 8.3-foot drop leaves 8.2 feet—often too short once you align a 21-inch pattern repeat! A 33-foot double roll yields three full 8-foot drops with minimal scrap.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a straight match and a drop match?
faqs.answer: In a straight match, the design lines up horizontally at the exact same height on every adjacent strip. In a drop (or half-drop) match, every other strip shifts down by half the pattern repeat height, creating a diagonal flow that uses 15%–20% more paper.

faqs.question: Can I hang peel-and-stick wallpaper over textured walls?
faqs.answer: Peel-and-stick vinyl requires a smooth surface. Over orange peel or knockdown texture, air pockets trap behind the adhesive and cause the vinyl to peel off within weeks. Skim-coat textured walls smooth or hang heavy non-woven paste-the-wall liner first.

faqs.question: How many rolls do I need for one 12×8 ft accent wall?
faqs.answer: A 12 ft × 8 ft accent wall is 96 sq ft. With 20% combined pattern and trim waste, you need 96 ÷ 25 × 1.20 = 4.6 single rolls, which rounds up to 3 double rolls.

name: Flooring Calculator (LVP, Laminate & Hardwood)
h1: Flooring Calculator: How Many Boxes of Flooring Do I Need?
intro: Calculate square footage, waste allowance, boxes of LVP, laminate, or hardwood planks, and rolls of underlayment for rectangular and L-shaped rooms.
metaTitle: Flooring Calculator: Sq Ft & Boxes (LVP, Wood) | BuildMath
metaDescription: Free flooring calculator for LVP, laminate, and hardwood. Supports L-shaped rooms, straight or diagonal waste %, box counts, and underlayment rolls.

inputs.name: sqFtPerBox
inputs.label: Coverage per Box
inputs.tooltip: Check the carton label: most LVP and laminate boxes contain 18.9 to 24.0 sq ft (20 sq ft industry average).

inputs.name: wastePercent
inputs.label: Layout & Cut Waste %
inputs.tooltip: NWFA & RFCI standard: 10% for straight lay, 15% for diagonal or herringbone patterns.

inputs.name: underlaymentRollSqFt
inputs.label: Underlayment Roll Size
inputs.tooltip: Standard residential acoustic/moisture barrier rolls cover 100 sq ft.

inputs.name: pricePerSqFt
inputs.label: Flooring Price per Sq Ft
inputs.tooltip: US retail 20-mil rigid-core LVP / laminate average ($2.29–$5.49/sq ft).

inputs.name: underlaymentPricePerRoll
inputs.label: Underlayment Price per Roll
inputs.tooltip: Average price for a 100 sq ft 3-in-1 foam/vapor underlayment roll.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Flooring Boxes Needed for Common Room Sizes (10% Waste, 20 sq ft/box)

howToCalculate.formula: Boxes = ceil( [ ((L1 × W1) + (L2 × W2)) × (1 + Waste%) ] ÷ Sq Ft per Box )
steps: Measure the length and width of your main room rectangle (L1 × W1).
If your room is L-shaped or has a walk-in closet, measure the second rectangle (L2 × W2) and add both areas together.
Multiply the net square footage by 1.10 for a standard straight installation (or 1.15 for a diagonal layout).
Divide the total square footage by the coverage per box printed on your flooring carton (typically 20 sq ft).
Always round UP to the next whole box so you have full planks for starter and finisher rows.

workedExample.title: Installing Click-Lock LVP in a 12×15 ft Living Room
workedExample.scenario: Your living room measures 15 ft × 12 ft, plus a 4 ft × 6 ft entry alcove. Your LVP boxes cover 20.1 sq ft each.
steps: Main Room = 15 × 12 = 180 sq ft; Entry Alcove = 6 × 4 = 24 sq ft.
Net Footprint = 180 + 24 = 204 sq ft.
Add 10% straight-lay waste = 204 × 1.10 = 224.4 sq ft.
Divide by box size = 224.4 ÷ 20.1 = 11.16 boxes.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 12 boxes of flooring (241.2 sq ft total) and 3 rolls of 100 sq ft underlayment.

tipsAndMistakes: Measure the last row width before starting Row 1: if your final wall row will be narrower than 2 inches, rip-cut your very first row narrower so both side walls have balanced, sturdy plank widths.
Stagger end joints by at least 6 to 8 inches: never line up short end seams in an "H-pattern" or stair-step pattern, which weakens the click-lock system and voids manufacturer warranties.

Leave a 1/4-inch to 3/8-inch expansion gap around every wall, pipe, and door jamb: floating floors expand and contract with seasonal temperature swings and will buckle if pinched tight against drywall.

Do not install a second foam pad under LVP that already has an attached pad—soft double padding causes click-lock joints to flex and snap underfoot. Over concrete, use a thin 6-mil poly vapor barrier instead.
Pull planks from 3 to 4 open boxes at the same time to randomize woodgrain print repeats and shade variations.
Undercut wood door casings with an oscillating multi-tool laying flat on a scrap plank so the flooring slides cleanly underneath the trim.

faqs.question: How many square feet are in a box of LVP or laminate flooring?
faqs.answer: Most luxury vinyl plank (LVP) and laminate cartons cover between 18.9 and 24.5 square feet (7 to 10 planks per box), with 20 sq ft being the most common benchmark. Engineered and solid 3/4-inch hardwood cartons typically cover 20 to 25 square feet.

faqs.question: Does LVP need to acclimate before installation?
faqs.answer: Rigid-core SPC vinyl planks usually require 24 to 48 hours of acclimation stacked flat in the room at 65°F–85°F. Laminate and solid hardwood require 48 to 72+ hours (and moisture meter testing for wood) so the planks adjust to your home’s indoor humidity.

faqs.question: How flat does my subfloor need to be for floating plank flooring?
faqs.answer: Nearly all LVP, laminate, and engineered wood manufacturers require the subfloor to be flat within 3/16 inch over a 10-foot span (or 1/8 inch over 6 feet). Grind down high humps and fill low dips with Portland-based floor patch before laying planks.

faqs.question: Should I remove baseboards or install quarter-round shoe moulding?
faqs.answer: Removing existing baseboards with a flat pry bar and reinstalling them 1/8 inch above the new floor gives the cleanest custom look. If your baseboards are glued or heavily caulked to fragile plaster, leave them in place and nail 3/4-inch quarter-round shoe moulding to the baseboard (never down into the floating floor).

faqs.question: How many extra boxes should I keep in storage after the project?
faqs.answer: Always keep 1 unopened box stored flat in a climate-controlled closet. Flooring manufacturers rotate patterns every 18 to 36 months, making it impossible to find matching click-lock profiles if a dishwasher leak or furniture gouge damages a plank later.

name: Tile Calculator (Floor, Shower & Backsplash)
h1: Tile Calculator: How Many Tiles, Boxes & Bags of Thinset Do I Need?
intro: Calculate exact tile count, boxes, 50-lb bags of thinset mortar, and grout for any floor, shower wall, or kitchen backsplash.
metaTitle: Tile Calculator: Tiles, Boxes & Thinset Mortar | BuildMath
metaDescription: Free tile calculator for floors, showers, and backsplashes. Enter room size, tile dimensions, and grout joint width to get tiles, boxes, and thinset.

inputs.name: groutJointInches
inputs.label: Grout Joint Width
inputs.tooltip: 1/16" (0.0625) for rectified porcelain, 1/8" (0.125) standard, 3/16"–1/4" for handmade or quarry tile.

inputs.name: tilesPerBox
inputs.label: Tiles per Box
inputs.tooltip: 12×24" boxes usually hold 6–8 tiles; 12×12" hold 10–15 tiles; 3×6" subway boxes hold 44–88 tiles.

inputs.name: thinsetCoverageSqFt
inputs.label: Thinset Coverage per 50-lb Bag
inputs.tooltip: A 50-lb bag covers ~85–95 sq ft with a 1/4×1/4" trowel, or ~50–65 sq ft with a 1/2×1/2" trowel + back-buttering.

inputs.name: wastePercent
inputs.label: Breakage & Cut Waste %
inputs.tooltip: TCNA standard: 10% for straight grid or 1/3 offset; 15% for diagonal, herringbone, or large-format tiles.

inputs.name: pricePerTile
inputs.label: Price per Single Tile
inputs.tooltip: Average price per tile ($3.25 for a 2 sq ft 12×24 tile ≈ $1.63/sq ft).

inputs.name: thinsetBagPrice
inputs.label: Thinset Mortar Price (50-lb Bag)
inputs.tooltip: US retail polymer-modified thinset mortar average ($18–$36/bag).

quickReferenceMeta.title: Tile, Box & Thinset Quantities for Common Projects (10% Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Tiles = ceil( [ (Area Sq Ft × 144) ÷ ((Tile W + Grout) × (Tile L + Grout)) ] × (1 + Waste%) )
steps: Multiply your room or wall Length × Width in feet to get total square footage, then multiply by 144 to convert to square inches.
Add the grout joint width to both the tile width and tile length in inches, then multiply them together to get the effective area of one installed tile.
Divide the room area (in sq in) by the effective tile area (in sq in).
Multiply by 1.10 (for 10% straight-lay waste) or 1.15 (for diagonal/herringbone) and round up to the next whole tile.
Divide total tiles by the number of tiles per box and round up to full cartons.

workedExample.title: Tiling a 10×12 ft Bathroom Floor with 12×24" Porcelain Tile
workedExample.scenario: A 10 ft × 12 ft bathroom (120 sq ft) uses 12" × 24" tiles with 1/8" (0.125") grout lines, 8 tiles per box, and 10% waste.
steps: Room Area in Sq Inches = 120 sq ft × 144 = 17,280 sq in.
Single Tile + Grout Area = (12 + 0.125) × (24 + 0.125) = 292.52 sq in.
Boxes = ceil(65 ÷ 8) = 9 boxes; Thinset = ceil(120 ÷ 60) = 2 bags.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 9 boxes (72 tiles), 2 bags of 50-lb polymer-modified thinset, and 1 bag of 25-lb grout.

tipsAndMistakes: Use a maximum 33% (1/3) offset on 12×24" and wood-look plank tiles: the TCNA Handbook warns against 50% brick-bond offsets on tiles longer than 15 inches because kiln bowing in the center creates toe-stubbing lippage.

Back-butter every large-format tile: skimming a flat layer of thinset onto the back of each 12×24" tile guarantees the 80% mortar contact (95% in wet showers) required to prevent hollow corners from cracking.
Comb thinset ridges in one straight direction—never in swirls! Directional ridges allow trapped air to escape when you press and slide the tile back and forth.
Dry-lay your centerlines first: snap chalk lines so border cuts along opposite walls are equal and at least half a tile wide.
Never use premixed "mastic" adhesive on floors, in showers, or with tiles larger than 8×8"—mastic re-emulsifies in moisture and never dries under dense porcelain.
Use 100% silicone caulk (not cement grout) at all 90-degree inside corners and where tile meets tubs, cabinets, or thresholds.

faqs.question: How many 12×24 tiles do I need for 100 square feet?
faqs.answer: Each 12×24 inch tile covers 2 square feet. With 10% cutting and breakage waste, 100 square feet requires 55 tiles (typically 7 boxes at 8 tiles per box).

faqs.question: What size notched trowel do I need for floor vs. wall tile?
faqs.answer: Use a 3/16" V-notch trowel for small mosaics and 3×6" subway backsplash tiles; a 1/4" × 3/8" square-notch trowel for 8×8" to 12×12" tiles; and a 1/2" × 1/2" square-notch (or slant-ridge) trowel for 12×24" and larger tiles.

faqs.question: Do I need cement backer board or an uncoupling membrane over plywood?
faqs.answer: Yes—never set ceramic or porcelain tile directly onto bare plywood or OSB, which swells with humidity and cracks the tile. Install 1/4-inch cement board taped with alkali-resistant mesh tape, or a 1/8-inch polyethylene uncoupling membrane like Schluter Ditra.

faqs.question: How much extra tile should I add for herringbone or diagonal patterns?
faqs.answer: Diagonal (45-degree), chevron, and herringbone patterns require angled wet-saw cuts at every single perimeter wall, increasing off-cut scrap. Increase the Waste slider to 15% (or 20% in small rooms with many corners).

faqs.question: What is the difference between ceramic and porcelain tile?
faqs.answer: Porcelain is fired at higher temperatures from refined kaolin clay, giving it a water absorption rate below 0.5% and through-body density ideal for floors, showers, and freezing patios. Standard ceramic is softer, easier to cut, and best suited for indoor walls and light-traffic bath floors.

inputs.label: Price per Bag
inputs.tooltip: US retail 25-lb polymer-modified grout average ($17–$34/bag).

quickReferenceMeta.title: Grout Required per 100 Sq Ft by Tile & Joint Size (3/8" Thick Tile)

howToCalculate.formula: Grout Lbs = [ ((L + W) ÷ (L × W)) × Joint Width × Joint Depth × 144 ÷ 1728 ] × Area Sq Ft × 100 lb/ft³ × (1 + Waste%)
steps: Add Tile Length + Tile Width and divide by (Tile Length × Tile Width) to find the linear joint ratio per square inch.
Multiply by the Grout Joint Width (in inches) and Tile Thickness (in inches) × 144 to get cubic inches of grout per square foot.
Multiply by your Total Tiled Area (sq ft) and divide by 1,728 to convert cubic inches into cubic feet.
Multiply cubic feet by 100 lbs/cu ft (standard cement grout density) and add 10% cleanup waste.
Divide total pounds by your chosen bag size (10 lb or 25 lb) and round up.

workedExample.title: Grouting 100 sq ft of 3×6" Subway Tile vs. 12×24" Floor Tile
workedExample.scenario: Compare 100 sq ft of 3×6" tile (1/8" joint, 1/4" thick) against 100 sq ft of 12×24" tile (1/8" joint, 3/8" thick).
steps: For 3×6" tile: Joint Ratio = (3 + 6) ÷ (3 × 6) = 0.50. Grout = 15.3 lbs (two 10-lb boxes or one 25-lb bag).
For 12×24" tile: Joint Ratio = (12 + 24) ÷ (12 × 24) = 0.125. Grout = 5.4 lbs (one 10-lb box).
Smaller tiles have 4× more linear joint footage per square foot and use nearly 3× as much grout!
workedExample.finalAnswer: Use 16 lbs for 100 sq ft of 3×6" tile, or 6 lbs for 100 sq ft of 12×24" tile.

tipsAndMistakes: Use unsanded grout for joints narrower than 1/8 inch: sand aggregate cannot pack tightly into 1/16" joints and will scratch polished marble or glass tiles.
Use sanded (or fine-aggregate high-performance) grout for joints 1/8 inch and wider: unsanded grout shrinks and cracks as water evaporates from wide joints.
Mix with cool, clean water and let the grout "slake" (rest in the bucket for 5–10 minutes, then remix without adding more water) so polymer crystals fully dissolve.
Hold your rubber grout float at a 45-degree angle and sweep diagonally across the tiles—sweeping parallel to the joint digs the wet grout right back out.
Wring your sponge nearly bone-dry during cleanup: flooding fresh grout with excess water washes pigment to the top and causes chalky white efflorescence blotches.
Wait 48 to 72 hours after grouting before applying a penetrating sealer (unless using pre-sealed urethane or epoxy grout).

faqs.question: Why do small mosaic tiles use so much more grout than large tiles?
faqs.answer: A 2×2-inch mosaic sheet has 12 linear feet of grout lines in every single square foot of tile, whereas a 12×24-inch tile has only 1.5 linear feet of grout lines per square foot—an 800% difference in joint volume.

faqs.question: When should I use sanded vs. unsanded grout?
faqs.answer: Follow the 1/8-inch rule: for narrow joints under 1/8" (such as rectified porcelain or glass backsplash tile), use unsanded grout. For joints 1/8" to 1/2" wide, use sanded grout so the silica sand prevents shrinkage cracking. Alternatively, modern calcium-aluminate grouts (like Custom Prism or Mapei Ultracolor Plus FA) work from 1/16" to 1/2".

faqs.question: How long should I wait after setting tile before grouting?
faqs.answer: Wait at least 24 hours after setting tiles in standard polymer-modified thinset mortar before walking on the floor or grouting. Grouting too early traps moisture from the thinset beneath the grout, leading to dark uneven curing.

faqs.question: Is epoxy or premixed urethane grout worth the extra cost?
faqs.answer: In heavy-use shower pans and kitchen countertops, epoxy or single-component urethane grout is non-porous, stain-proof, and never needs sealing—though it costs 3× more per bucket and requires faster sponge cleanup.

faqs.question: How do I fix grout that dried lighter or blotchy in spots?
faqs.answer: Blotchy light spots are usually polymer haze or efflorescence caused by using too much water during sponge cleanup. Scrub with a sulfamic-acid grout haze remover after 7 days, or apply a 2-in-1 grout colorant and sealer.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Carpet Square Yards & 12-Ft Roll Lengths for Common Room Sizes (10% Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Square Yards = ceil( [ Length × Width × (1 + Waste%) ] ÷ 9 ); Roll Length = Total Sq Ft ÷ 12 ft
steps: Multiply Room Length × Room Width in feet to get net square footage.
Multiply by 1.10 to add a 10% allowance for broadloom roll width cuts and closets.
Divide total square feet by 9 (since 1 yard = 3 feet, and 3 ft × 3 ft = 9 sq ft per square yard).
To see how many linear feet a retailer will cut off a 12-foot roll, divide total square feet by 12.

workedExample.title: Carpeting a 12×15 ft Bedroom
workedExample.scenario: You are carpeting a 12 ft × 15 ft bedroom using standard 12-ft broadloom carpet priced at $27/sq yd and padding at $6.50/sq yd.
steps: Net Room Area = 15 ft × 12 ft = 180 sq ft.
With 10% waste (for closet & doorway turns) = 180 × 1.10 = 198 sq ft.
Square Yards = 198 ÷ 9 = 22 sq yd.
12-Ft Roll Cut = 198 ÷ 12 = 16.5 linear feet off the roll.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 22 square yards (198 sq ft) of carpet and 22 square yards of 8-lb rebond padding.

tipsAndMistakes: Always check the 12-foot roll rule: because carpet comes on a fixed 12-foot roll, a 13×15 ft room requires a full 12×15 cut PLUS a seamed 1-foot-wide strip ("fill piece"), using more yardage than simple square footage suggests.

Keep carpet pile nap running in the same direction across every seam and adjacent room—if two pieces are seamed with opposing pile angles, light reflects differently and makes the seam look like a two-tone color mismatch.
Upgrade the pad before upgrading the carpet: an 8-lb density, 7/16-inch thick rebond pad makes a mid-grade carpet feel plush and prevents fibers from crushing.
Never go thicker than 7/16-inch padding on residential tackless installations: 1/2-inch or thicker foam prevents carpet backing from hooking onto tack-strip pins and causes wrinkles.
Use a power stretcher (not just a knee kicker): CRI 105 standards mandate power-stretching carpet wall-to-wall so ripples never form in humid weather.
Count stair steps separately: each standard box step takes a 2-foot-long by 3.5-foot-wide piece of carpet (0.78 sq yd per step).

faqs.question: How do you convert square feet to square yards for carpet?
faqs.answer: Divide your total square footage by 9 (never by 3!). Because a yard is 3 feet long by 3 feet wide, 1 square yard equals 9 square feet. For example, 180 sq ft ÷ 9 = 20 square yards.

faqs.question: Why is a 13×13 ft room more expensive to carpet than a 12×14 ft room?
faqs.answer: A 12×14 ft room fits seamlessly onto a single 14-foot cut from a 12-foot-wide roll (168 sq ft). A 13×13 ft room is 1 foot wider than the 12-foot roll, forcing the installer to buy an extra 4 to 6 linear feet off the roll to cut and seam the 1-foot-wide side strip.

faqs.question: What density and thickness of carpet pad is best?
faqs.answer: For bedrooms, living rooms, and stairs, the Carpet and Rug Institute (CRI) and major mills recommend an 8-pound density, 7/16-inch (or 3/8-inch for berber/loop pile) rebond urethane foam pad with a top spill moisture barrier.

faqs.question: How much carpet do I need for a flight of 13 stairs?
faqs.answer: A standard 13-step staircase (36 inches wide) requires roughly 9 to 10 square yards (80 to 90 sq ft) of carpet and padding, with the pile direction always running downward from top to bottom.

faqs.question: Nylon vs. Polyester (PET) vs. Triexta carpet: which lasts longest?
faqs.answer: Nylon has the highest fiber resiliency and bounce-back for high-traffic stairs and hallways. Solution-dyed polyester (PET) is budget-friendly and naturally stain-resistant for bedrooms, while Triexta (SmartStrand) blends high stain resistance with strong durability.

inputs.tooltip: Standard interior doors + casing width deduct ~3 linear feet per doorway.

inputs.name: boardLengthFeet
inputs.label: Baseboard Stock Length
inputs.tooltip: Home centers stock 8-ft, 12-ft, and 16-ft lengths. Longer boards mean fewer scarf joints.

inputs.tooltip: Primed MDF/pine 3.25"–5.25" baseboard averages $1.25–$3.20 per linear foot.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Baseboard Pieces Needed by Room Perimeter (10% Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Boards = ceil( [ (Room Perimeter − (Doors × Door Width)) × (1 + Waste%) ] ÷ Board Length )
steps: Add the length of all walls in the room (plus inside closets if trimming them) to get the gross Room Perimeter.
Subtract 3 feet for each standard single doorway (or 5–6 feet for double bifold closet doors).
Multiply net linear footage by 1.10 to account for 10% miter and off-cut waste.
Divide by your chosen stock board length (8 ft, 12 ft, or 16 ft) and round up to whole boards.

workedExample.title: Trimming a 12×15 ft Bedroom (54 ft Perimeter)
workedExample.scenario: A 12 ft × 15 ft bedroom has a 54-ft perimeter and 2 doorways (3 ft each). You are buying 12-ft primed pine boards.
steps: Net Perimeter = 54 ft − (2 × 3 ft) = 48 linear feet.
Add 10% miter waste = 48 × 1.10 = 52.8 linear feet.
Divide by 12-ft board length = 52.8 ÷ 12 = 4.4 boards.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Buy 5 boards at 12-ft length (or 7 boards at 8-ft length) plus 2 tubes of paintable caulk.

tipsAndMistakes: Buy 12-ft or 16-ft boards whenever possible: spanning an entire 12-foot bedroom wall with a single board eliminates ugly mid-wall scarf joints.

Cope inside corners instead of mitering: drywall corners are rarely an exact 90 degrees (mud build-up makes them 88°–89°); cutting one board square and coping the profile of the mating board with a coping saw guarantees a tight joint that never opens in winter.
Cut outside corners at 45.5 or 46 degrees: because drywall corner bead flares out slightly, a 46-degree miter keeps the front tip of the outside corner tight.
Pre-prime and apply two coats of semi-gloss trim paint on sawhorses BEFORE nailing the baseboards to the wall—then you only have to touch up nail holes and the top caulk line.
Nail into wall studs (spaced 16" OC) using 2-inch 16-gauge or 18-gauge finish nails, hitting both the bottom plate and each vertical stud.
Never caulk the bottom gap between baseboard and hardwood/LVP flooring: the floor needs to move independently; only caulk the top seam against the drywall.

faqs.question: Should I choose MDF or solid pine/poplar baseboard?
faqs.answer: Primed MDF (medium-density fiberboard) is cheap, knot-free, and flexible enough to hug slightly wavy walls in living rooms and bedrooms. However, MDF swells like cardboard if it gets wet—always use solid primed pine, poplar, or PVC trim in bathrooms, laundry rooms, and kitchens.

faqs.question: What height baseboard looks best with 8-ft vs. 9-ft ceilings?
faqs.answer: For standard 8-foot ceilings, 3-1/4 inch to 4-1/4 inch baseboard is proportional. For 9-foot or 10-foot ceilings, upgrade to 5-1/4 inch or 7-1/4 inch tall baseboard so the trim doesn’t look undersized.

faqs.question: How do I join two baseboard pieces on a wall longer than 16 feet?
faqs.answer: Use a 45-degree overlapping "scarf joint" positioned directly over a wall stud. Put a dab of wood glue between the overlapping 45-degree bevels, nail through both pieces into the stud, and sand flush before painting.

faqs.question: What gauge nailer is best for baseboard and shoe moulding?
faqs.answer: A 16-gauge finish nailer with 2-inch nails has the holding power to pull thick 9/16" baseboards tight against drywall into wood studs. Use an 18-gauge brad nailer with 1-1/2" brads for thinner MDF trim, door casings, and quarter-round shoe moulding.

faqs.question: Do I install baseboards before or after new flooring?
faqs.answer: Install baseboards AFTER laying hardwood, LVP, laminate, or tile so the bottom edge of the baseboard covers the 1/4-inch perimeter expansion gap without needing extra quarter-round shoe moulding. For wall-to-wall carpet, install baseboards first elevated 3/8 inch off the subfloor so the carpet tucks underneath.

inputs.name: wastePercent

quickReferenceMeta.title: Concrete Yards & 80-Lb Bags for Common Slab Sizes (4" Thick + 10% Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Cubic Feet = L × W × (Thickness_in ÷ 12) × (1 + Waste%); Cubic Yards = Cu Ft ÷ 27; 80-lb Bags = ceil(Cu Ft ÷ 0.60)
steps: Convert your slab thickness from inches to feet by dividing by 12 (for example, 4 inches ÷ 12 = 0.333 feet).
Multiply Length (ft) × Width (ft) × Thickness (ft) to get net volume in Cubic Feet.
Add 10% waste (multiply by 1.10) to account for uneven gravel base and form bowing.
Divide Cubic Feet by 27 to convert to Cubic Yards (for ordering a ready-mix truck).
For bagged concrete, divide Cubic Feet by 0.60 for 80-lb bags (or 0.45 for 60-lb bags, 0.30 for 40-lb bags).

workedExample.title: Pouring a 10×12 ft Backyard Patio Slab (4 Inches Thick)
workedExample.scenario: You are pouring a 10 ft × 12 ft concrete patio at 4 inches thick with a 10% subgrade waste buffer.
steps: Net Cubic Feet = 12 ft × 10 ft × (4 ÷ 12 ft) = 40.0 cu ft.
With 10% waste = 40.0 × 1.10 = 44.0 cu ft.
Cubic Yards = 44.0 ÷ 27 = 1.63 cubic yards.
80-lb Bags = ceil(44.0 ÷ 0.60) = 74 bags (or 98 bags of 60-lb mix).
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 1.75 cubic yards of ready-mix concrete, or buy 74 bags of 80-lb concrete mix.

tipsAndMistakes: Remember that a nominal 2×4 form board is actually 3.5 inches tall—not 4 inches! If you want a true 4-inch slab, use 2×6 form boards staked and marked at 4 inches, or excavate 1/2 inch below the 2×4 forms.
Never add extra water to make concrete easier to rake: raising the water-to-cement ratio slashes compressive strength from 4,000 PSI down to 2,200 PSI and causes surface flaking (spalling).

Cut contraction control joints every 8 to 10 feet: concrete always shrinks as it cures; grooving or saw-cutting joints to 1/4 of the slab thickness (1 inch deep on a 4" slab) forces cracks to hide neatly inside the joint.
Wait until the metallic "bleed water" sheen disappears from the surface before floating or troweling—working bleed water back into the top paste guarantees scaling.
Over 1.5 cubic yards (~68 bags of 80-lb mix), ordering a ready-mix truck or towable U-Cart is cheaper and eliminates cold joints.
Keep fresh concrete damp or spray it with acrylic cure-and-seal compound immediately after broom-finishing so it reaches full 28-day strength.

faqs.question: How many 80-lb or 60-lb bags of concrete equal 1 cubic yard?
faqs.answer: One cubic yard equals 27 cubic feet. Because an 80-lb bag yields 0.60 cubic feet, it takes exactly 45 bags of 80-lb concrete to make 1 cubic yard. A 60-lb bag yields 0.45 cubic feet, requiring 60 bags per cubic yard, while a 40-lb bag requires 90 bags per cubic yard.

faqs.question: How thick should a concrete patio vs. driveway slab be?
faqs.answer: A backyard patio, shed pad, or sidewalk supporting foot traffic should be 4 inches thick over 4 inches of compacted crushed stone. A residential driveway supporting SUVs and pickup trucks should be 4 to 5 inches thick, and an RV or heavy dump-truck pad should be 6 inches thick with #4 rebar.

faqs.question: How much water do I add to an 80-lb bag of concrete?
faqs.answer: Start with 3 quarts (0.75 gallons) of clean water per 80-lb bag. If needed, add up to 1 additional pint for a workable 4-inch slump, never exceeding 3.5 quarts per bag.

faqs.question: Do I need wire mesh or rebar in a 4-inch concrete slab?
faqs.answer: While fibers or wire mesh help hold hairline shrinkage cracks together, #3 or #4 steel rebar on 18-inch centers supported on 2-inch plastic chairs provides far superior structural load transfer across freeze-thaw movement and tree roots.

faqs.question: How long before I can walk or drive on a new concrete slab?
faqs.answer: You can walk carefully on new concrete after 24 to 48 hours. Wait at least 7 days before parking passenger cars on a new driveway, and wait a full 28 days before parking heavy trucks, trailers, or RVs.

steps: Divide the tube diameter in inches by 2 to get the radius in inches, then divide by 12 to convert the radius into feet.
Square the radius (r × r), multiply by π (3.1416), and multiply by the depth in feet (Depth_in ÷ 12) to get the volume of 1 pier.

workedExample.title: Pouring Four 12-Inch Deck Piers at 42 Inches Deep
workedExample.scenario: Your building code requires 12-inch diameter piers extending 42 inches (3.5 ft) deep for 4 deck support posts.
steps: Radius in feet = (12 in ÷ 2) ÷ 12 = 0.50 ft.
Single Pier Volume = 3.1416 × (0.50)² × 3.5 ft = 2.75 cu ft.
80-lb Bags = ceil(12.10 ÷ 0.60) = 21 bags (~5.2 bags per pier).
workedExample.finalAnswer: Buy 21 bags of 80-lb concrete mix and four 12-inch forming tubes.

tipsAndMistakes: Always set wood posts ON TOP of the concrete pier using an elevated galvanized post base (like a Simpson ABU44 or ABA66)—embedding wood posts inside wet concrete traps water and rots the post at ground level.
Extend your Sonotube 4 to 6 inches ABOVE finished soil grade so rainwater and lawnmowers stay clear of the wood post.
Bell out the bottom of the hole if required by soil bearing code, or use a snap-on plastic footing base (Bigfoot / Redibase) under the cardboard tube.
Drop two vertical #4 rebar rods into each pier (held 3 inches off the dirt bottom) to prevent frost heave from shearing the column.
Tap the sides of the Sonotube with a rubber mallet or rod the wet mix with a 2×2 stick as you pour to eliminate honeycomb air pockets.
Wait for the building inspector to approve your open holes BEFORE pouring concrete!

faqs.question: How many 80-lb bags of concrete does one 12-inch × 48-inch Sonotube take?
faqs.answer: A 12-inch diameter by 48-inch (4-foot) tall cylinder has an exact volume of 3.14 cubic feet. Divided by 0.60 cu ft per 80-lb bag, one tube takes 5.24 bags—so buy 6 bags of 80-lb concrete (or 7 bags of 60-lb concrete) per tube.

faqs.question: How deep do deck footings need to be?
faqs.answer: IRC code requires deck footings to extend at least 12 inches below undisturbed soil AND below your local frost line (which ranges from 12" in the South to 36"–48" in the Midwest/Northeast and 60"+ in Minnesota). Freestanding small sheds sometimes qualify for frost-protected shallow foundations.

faqs.question: Do I need to peel the cardboard Sonotube off after the concrete dries?
faqs.answer: You only need to peel away the top 4 to 6 inches of cardboard that stick up above ground level so it looks clean. Below ground, the wax-treated cardboard can remain in place.

faqs.question: Should I put gravel in the bottom of a deck footing hole?
faqs.answer: Ask your local building inspector first: for fence posts set directly in the ground, 4 inches of gravel aids drainage. However, for structural deck piers, many inspectors require concrete to bear directly on undisturbed native soil without loose gravel underneath.

faqs.question: When do I insert the J-bolt anchor into the pier?
faqs.answer: Push a 1/2" × 8" galvanized J-bolt (or wet-set post base) into the center of the wet concrete immediately after screeding the top of the tube flat, leaving the threaded portion protruding to bolt down your adjustable post base.

name: Concrete Steps Calculator
h1: Concrete Steps Calculator: How Much Concrete for Stairs & Landing?

quickReferenceMeta.title: Concrete Needed for Common Exterior Steps (7.5" Rise × 11" Tread)

howToCalculate.formula: Volume (cu ft) = Width × [ (Rise_ft × Tread_ft × N × (N + 1) ÷ 2) + (N × Rise_ft × Landing_ft) ] × (1 + Waste%)
steps: Convert Riser Height and Tread Depth from inches to feet (divide each by 12).
Calculate the volume of a single bottom step block: Stair Width × Riser_ft × Tread_ft.
Because Step 2 is 2 risers tall, Step 3 is 3 risers tall, and Step N is N risers tall, multiply the single-step volume by N × (N + 1) ÷ 2.
Add the Top Landing volume: Stair Width × (N × Riser_ft) × Landing Depth.
Add 10% waste and divide by 27 for cubic yards (or divide by 0.60 for 80-lb bags).

workedExample.title: Pouring 3 Steps (4 ft Wide) with a 3-ft Top Landing
workedExample.scenario: You are pouring 3 steps (7.5" rise, 11" tread, 4 ft wide) plus a 3-ft deep top landing.
steps: 1-Step Unit Volume = 4 ft × (7.5 ÷ 12) × (11 ÷ 12) = 2.292 cu ft.
Steps Total (1 + 2 + 3 = 6 units) = 2.292 × 6 = 13.75 cu ft.
Top Landing Volume = 4 ft × (3 × 0.625 ft) × 3 ft = 22.50 cu ft.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 1.5 cubic yards of ready-mix, or buy 67 bags of 80-lb concrete (save concrete by filling the hollow center core with compacted crushed stone/CMU blocks).

tipsAndMistakes: Save 40% of your concrete on tall landings by building an inner core of compacted crushed gravel or CMU cinder blocks under the top landing so the poured concrete shell is 6 inches thick rather than solid concrete all the way down.
Bevel the bottom edge of each wood riser form board at a 45-degree angle facing inward so your steel finishing trowel can reach all the way to the back corner of every tread.
Mix concrete slightly stiffer (3-inch slump) when pouring steps: soupy concrete slumps out the bottom of the lower riser forms when you fill the upper steps.
Brace riser forms heavily with 2×4 kickers staked into the ground—wet concrete weighs 150 lbs per cubic foot and will bow unbraced 3/4" plywood.
Strip the vertical riser face forms carefully after 4 to 6 hours (while the concrete is "green" and firm) so you can rub out bug holes and bullnose the step edges with a step edger.
Slope each tread 1/8 inch forward per foot so rainwater and melting ice drain off the steps.

faqs.question: Do concrete steps need to be solid all the way through?
faqs.answer: Small 2-step or 3-step stoops are often poured solid, but for 4+ steps with a deep landing, pouring solid concrete wastes money and adds immense weight. Fill the interior cavity with compacted #57 crushed stone in 4-inch tamped lifts, leaving a 6-inch concrete thickness beneath the treads and landing.

faqs.question: How do I attach new concrete steps to my house foundation?
faqs.answer: If your steps sit on their own frost-depth footings, drill and epoxy #4 rebar dowels into the foundation wall. If pouring a floating stoop on a gravel pad in a freeze-thaw climate, isolate it from the house wall with 1/2-inch expansion joint board so frost heave doesn’t crack the wall.

faqs.question: What is the building code for exterior concrete step height and depth?
faqs.answer: Under IRC Section R311.7.5, the maximum riser height is 7-3/4 inches (7.75"), the minimum tread depth is 10 inches, and the tallest riser cannot vary from the shortest riser by more than 3/8 inch across the entire flight.

faqs.question: When should I broom-finish concrete steps?
faqs.answer: Pull a damp medium-bristle concrete broom across each tread perpendicular to the direction of travel right after edging and floating, once surface bleed water has evaporated. This creates non-slip traction ridges for wet or icy shoes.

faqs.question: Do exterior steps require a handrail?
faqs.answer: Yes—under IRC Section R311.7.8, any stairway with 4 or more risers requires a continuous graspable handrail (34 to 38 inches high) on at least one side.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Bricks & 80-Lb Mortar Bags for Common Wall Sizes (Modular Brick + 5% Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Bricks = ceil( (Wall Length × Height − Openings) × 6.75 × (1 + Waste%) ); Mortar Bags = ceil(Bricks ÷ 35)
steps: Multiply Wall Length × Wall Height in feet and subtract any window or door openings to get Net Wall Square Footage.
Multiply Net Sq Ft by 6.75 (for standard modular bricks laid with a 3/8-inch mortar joint in a single-wythe veneer).
Multiply by 1.05 to add a 5% allowance for half-brick end cuts and pallet breakage.
Divide your total brick count by 35 to find how many 80-lb bags of pre-mixed Type N masonry mortar you need.

workedExample.title: Building a 20-ft × 4-ft Brick Garden Knee Wall
workedExample.scenario: You are laying a single-wythe 20 ft × 4 ft modular brick veneer wall (80 sq ft) with 3/8-inch mortar joints and 5% waste.
steps: Wall Area = 20 × 4 = 80 sq ft.
Net Bricks = 80 × 6.75 = 540 bricks.
With 5% waste = 540 × 1.05 = 567 bricks.
Mortar Bags = ceil(567 ÷ 35) = 17 bags of 80-lb Type N mortar.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 567 modular bricks (approx. 1.15 pallets) and 17 bags of 80-lb Type N mortar.

tipsAndMistakes: Double your brick count for a freestanding double-wythe structural brick wall: the 6.75 bricks/sq ft factor is for a single layer (wythe) of brick veneer.
Use Type N mortar for above-grade exterior walls and veneers, and Type S mortar for below-grade foundations or freestanding retaining pillars.
Never use concrete mix (which contains coarse gravel) to lay bricks! Always buy "Mason Mix" or "Mortar Mix" made with fine masonry sand and hydrated lime.
Wait until the mortar is "thumbprint hard" before striking the joints with a concave jointer tool—tooling wet mortar smears gray stains onto the red brick face.
Install weep holes (every 24 to 33 inches along the bottom course) and corrugated galvanized wall ties (1 tie per 2.67 sq ft) on all wood-framed brick veneers.
Blend bricks from 3 pallets simultaneously so natural kiln color variations distribute evenly across the wall.

faqs.question: How many standard bricks are in a square foot?
faqs.answer: According to the Brick Industry Association (BIA), standard modular bricks (measuring 3-5/8" deep × 2-1/4" high × 7-5/8" long) laid with a 3/8-inch mortar joint require 6.75 bricks per square foot. With a wider 1/2-inch mortar joint, you need 6.16 bricks per square foot.

faqs.question: How many bricks does one 80-lb bag of mortar lay?
faqs.answer: One 80-lb bag of pre-blended Type N mortar mix lays approximately 33 to 38 standard modular bricks (or 12 to 14 standard 8×8×16 concrete cinder blocks) with a 3/8-inch joint. A 60-lb bag lays roughly 25 to 28 bricks.

faqs.question: How many bricks are on a full pallet or cube?
faqs.answer: A standard residential brick cube (strapped bundle) typically holds 500 to 525 modular bricks and weighs roughly 2,000 to 2,200 pounds.

faqs.question: Should I wet bricks before laying them?
faqs.answer: If a drop of water drawn on a dry clay brick with a wax pencil disappears in less than 60 seconds, mist the brick pallet with a hose a few hours before laying so dry bricks remained surface-dry but internally damp—otherwise dry clay sucks water out of the mortar and kills bond strength.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Type N and Type S mortar?
faqs.answer: Type N mortar (~750 PSI) is medium-strength and slightly flexible, making it ideal for above-grade brick veneer and chimneys because if thermal movement occurs, the mortar joint yields rather than cracking the brick. Type S (~1,800 PSI) is higher-strength for below-grade or structural masonry.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Pavers, Gravel Base (4") & Sand (1") for Common Patio Sizes (4×8" Pavers)

howToCalculate.formula: Pavers = ceil( [ Area ÷ (Paver_L × Paver_W ÷ 144) ] × (1 + Waste%) ); Gravel Tons = (Area × (Base_in ÷ 12) ÷ 27) × 1.4
steps: Multiply Patio Length × Width to find your patio surface area in square feet.
Calculate the face area of 1 paver in square feet: (Paver Length_in × Paver Width_in) ÷ 144.
Divide Patio Area by Single Paver Area and add 5%–10% waste for border cuts.
Calculate Crushed Gravel Base: Area × (4" or 6" ÷ 12) ÷ 27 = Cubic Yards; multiply by 1.4 tons/cu yd for weight.
Calculate Bedding Sand: Area × (1" ÷ 12) ÷ 27 = Cubic Yards; multiply by 1.35 tons/cu yd for weight.

workedExample.title: Building a 12×16 ft Patio (192 sq ft) with 4×8" Brick Pavers
workedExample.scenario: You are installing a 12 ft × 16 ft patio using 4" × 8" pavers, a 4-inch gravel base, a 1-inch sand bed, and 10% paver waste.
steps: Patio Area = 16 × 12 = 192 sq ft.
Single 4×8" Paver Area = 32 ÷ 144 = 0.2222 sq ft (4.5 pavers per sq ft).
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 951 pavers, 3.32 tons (2.37 yd³) of crusher-run gravel, 0.80 tons (0.59 yd³) of C-33 sand, and 3 bags of polymeric sand.

tipsAndMistakes: Never use round pea gravel for a paver base: round stones roll like marbles under load. Always ask for "crusher run", "dense grade aggregate (DGA)", "road base", or "#411 crushed limestone" containing angular rock mixed with stone dust fines.
Never screed bedding sand thicker than 1 inch (and never use sand to fill low spots in your gravel!): thick sand pockets compress under patio chairs and leave sunken dips.
Excavate 6 inches wider than your finished paver footprint on all open sides so your plastic edge restraints sit on solid compacted gravel rather than crumbling dirt.
Compact your gravel base in two separate 2-inch lifts with a vibrating plate compactor, misting lightly with water on each pass.
Blow every grain of polymeric sand off the top of the pavers with a leaf blower BEFORE misting with water so polymer resin never hazes the stone surface.
Slope the patio 1/8" to 1/4" per foot away from your house foundation.

faqs.question: How many 4×8 pavers do I need per square foot?
faqs.answer: A standard 4×8-inch brick paver covers 32 square inches, so it takes exactly 4.5 pavers to cover 1 square foot (before adding 5% to 10% for cutting waste). A 6×6-inch paver takes 4 per sq ft, and a 12×12-inch patio slab takes 1 per sq ft.

faqs.question: Are foam paver base panels better than 4 inches of crushed gravel?
faqs.answer: Interlocking polypropylene paver base panels (like Brock PaverBase) save digging 4 inches of dirt on small flat walkways in mild climates. However, in freeze-thaw states, heavy clay soils, or large patios, a 4-to-6-inch compacted crushed stone base is far more stable and cheaper per square foot.

faqs.question: What is the difference between bedding sand and polymeric sand?
faqs.answer: Bedding sand is coarse, washed ASTM C33 concrete sand screeded in a 1-inch layer underneath the pavers. Polymeric sand is fine sand blended with water-activated polymer binders that is swept into the vertical cracks between pavers at the very end to lock them together.

faqs.question: How deep do I need to dig for a paver patio?
faqs.answer: Add your base depth (4" or 6") + bedding sand (1") + paver thickness (typically 2-3/8" for standard pavers or 1-3/4" for patio slabs). That equals 7-3/8 inches total excavation depth for a 4-inch base, or 9-3/8 inches for a 6-inch freeze-thaw base.

faqs.question: How many square feet does a 50-lb bag of polymeric sand cover?
faqs.answer: One 50-lb bag of polymeric joint sand covers roughly 50 to 75 square feet for standard 4×8 pavers with narrow joints, or 85 to 120 square feet for large-format patio slabs.

inputs.name: blockHeightInches
inputs.label: Block Course Height

inputs.label: Add 1 Buried Base Course Below Ground?
inputs.tooltip: NCMA guidelines require burying at least the first course (or 10% of wall height) below grade to prevent toe kick-out.

inputs.name: wastePercent
inputs.label: Corner & Cut Waste %
inputs.tooltip: 5% standard allowance for half-block stagger cuts and curves.

inputs.label: Price per Wall Block
inputs.tooltip: US retail 6×16" interlocking retaining wall block average ($3.85–$7.95).

inputs.name: pricePerCapBlock
inputs.label: Price per Cap Block
inputs.tooltip: Flat top cap stone average.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Retaining Wall Blocks & Caps for Common Wall Sizes (6×16" Blocks + Buried Row)

howToCalculate.formula: Blocks per Row = ceil((Wall Length_ft × 12) ÷ Block Length_in); Total Rows = ceil((Height_ft × 12) ÷ Block Height_in) + 1 Buried Row
steps: Convert Wall Length to inches (Length_ft × 12) and divide by the Block Length in inches to get Blocks per Row.
Convert Exposed Wall Height to inches (Height_ft × 12) and divide by Block Height in inches to get Exposed Rows.
Add 1 extra row for the buried base course below soil grade (essential so soil pressure cannot push the bottom row forward).
Multiply Blocks per Row × Total Rows and add 5% waste.
Add 1 row of Cap Blocks plus 12 inches of #57 washed drainage gravel behind the entire height of the wall.

workedExample.title: Building a 25-ft Long × 3-ft High Retaining Wall (6×16" Blocks)
workedExample.scenario: You are building a 25-ft long wall with 3 ft exposed height using 6" H × 16" L blocks, including 1 buried base row and 5% waste.
steps: Blocks per Row = ceil((25 × 12) ÷ 16) = ceil(18.75) = 19 blocks.
Exposed Rows = ceil((3 × 12) ÷ 6) = 6 rows + 1 buried row = 7 total courses.
Wall Blocks w/ 5% waste = 19 × 7 × 1.05 = 139.65 → 140 blocks.
Cap Blocks w/ 5% waste = ceil(19 × 1.05) = 20 cap blocks.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 140 retaining wall blocks, 20 cap blocks, 2 tubes of landscape adhesive, and 4.54 tons (3.24 yd³) of #57 drainage gravel.

tipsAndMistakes: Take 60% of your project time on Row 1: if your buried base course is dead level front-to-back and side-to-side on 6 inches of compacted crusher-run, stacking the upper rows takes minutes.
Knock the rear interlocking lip off the first buried base row (with a mason hammer) so the blocks sit flat on your compacted leveling pad.

Never backfill directly behind a retaining wall with dirt or clay! Wet clay expands and creates hydrostatic water pressure that pushes walls over. Always fill a 12-inch column directly behind the blocks with clean, washed #57 angular drainage stone and a 4-inch perforated drain pipe at the base.
Separate the washed drainage gravel from the native soil behind it using non-woven landscape filter fabric so dirt cannot clog the stone voids.
Stagger vertical joints in a running bond (half-block offset) and glue the top cap blocks down with exterior polyurethane landscape block adhesive.

Check local building codes: most cities require a building permit, stamped engineering, and geogrid tieback fabric for any retaining wall over 4 feet tall (measured from the bottom of the footing to the top of the cap).

faqs.question: Why do I need to bury the first row of retaining wall blocks?
faqs.answer: The earth behind a retaining wall pushes forward with tremendous lateral force at the base. Burying at least one full block course (or 1 inch per 8 inches of wall height) creates a passive soil "toe" in front of the wall that prevents the bottom row from sliding out.

faqs.question: What is the maximum height for a DIY gravity retaining wall without geogrid?
faqs.answer: Most residential 6×16-inch bevel blocks are engineered for gravity walls up to 3.0 to 3.5 feet tall without reinforcement. Above 3.5 to 4.0 feet, you must embed horizontal layers of bi-axial geogrid mesh extending 4 to 6 feet back into the compacted backfill.

faqs.question: What kind of gravel goes under the base vs. behind the wall?
faqs.answer: Use two different gravels: UNDER the first course, use 6 inches of compactable "crusher run" or road base (which has stone dust fines that pack rock-hard). BEHIND the wall, use clean, washed 3/4-inch angular stone (#57 stone) with zero fines so water drains freely into the perforated pipe.

faqs.question: Which way do the holes in a perforated drain pipe face?
faqs.answer: Place the 4-inch rigid PVC drain pipe with the two rows of holes facing DOWNWARD (at the 4 o’clock and 8 o’clock positions) on a 2-inch bed of gravel. As groundwater rises in the gravel trench, it enters the bottom holes and flows out to daylight without washing silt into the pipe.

faqs.question: How do I cut concrete retaining wall blocks for half-blocks and curves?
faqs.answer: Score a 1.5-inch-deep line all the way around the block using a 7-inch circular saw or angle grinder fitted with a segmented diamond masonry blade, then strike the score line sharply with a 3-lb drilling hammer and brick chisel.

quickReferenceMeta.title: 20-Ft Rebar Bars & Tie Intersections for Common Slab Sizes

howToCalculate.formula: Rows_L = floor((Width − 2×Clearance) ÷ Spacing) + 1; Rows_W = floor((Length − 2×Clearance) ÷ Spacing) + 1; Bars = ceil(Total Linear Ft × (1 + Overlap%) ÷ 20)
steps: Subtract 6 inches (3" concrete cover on each side) from both the Slab Length and Slab Width to get the net rebar mat dimensions.
Divide the net width by the On-Center Spacing (in feet) and add 1 to find the number of lengthwise bars.
Divide the net length by the On-Center Spacing (in feet) and add 1 to find the number of widthwise crossbars.
Multiply lengthwise bars × net length, and widthwise bars × net width, then add them together for Net Linear Feet.
Add 10% for lap-splice overlaps, then divide by 20 ft (or 10 ft) and round up to whole bars.

workedExample.title: Reinforcing a 20×20 ft Two-Car Garage Slab at 18" On-Center
workedExample.scenario: You are laying a #4 rebar grid at 18" OC in a 20 ft × 20 ft slab with 3" edge clearance and 20-ft bars.
steps: Net Mat Dimensions = 20 ft − 0.5 ft = 19.5 ft × 19.5 ft.
Runs Each Way = floor(19.5 ÷ 1.5 ft) + 1 = 13 + 1 = 14 bars lengthwise and 14 bars widthwise.
Net Linear Footage = (14 × 19.5) + (14 × 19.5) = 546 linear feet.
With 10% splice overlap = 546 × 1.10 = 600.6 linear feet.
20-Ft Bars = ceil(600.6 ÷ 20) = 31 bars; Intersections = 14 × 14 = 196 ties.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 31 bars of 20-ft #4 rebar, 200 wire loop ties, and 100 plastic rebar support chairs.

tipsAndMistakes: Rebar laying flat on the dirt does ZERO structural work! Always snap 2-inch plastic rebar chairs (or dobies) under the grid so the steel sits cleanly in the center of your 4-inch slab.
Overlap spliced rebar ends by 40 bar diameters: for #3 (3/8") rebar, overlap at least 15 inches; for #4 (1/2") rebar, overlap at least 20 inches and wire-tie the splice in two spots.
Keep all cut rebar ends at least 3 inches back from the wooden perimeter forms—if steel touches the outside edge of the slab, moisture wicks in, rusts the bar, and pops the corner off.
Use pre-looped 6-inch annealed wire ties with a $12 spring-loaded pull-twister tool to tie a 200-intersection grid in under 30 minutes without blistering your wrists.
You only need to tie every other intersection (checkerboard pattern) on flat slabs—tie wire just holds the grid in place during the pour; it adds no structural strength once concrete cures.
Add two diagonal 3-foot "re-entrant corner bars" at any inside L-shape corner or around floor drain cutouts where shrinkage cracks always start.

faqs.question: Should I use #3 (3/8") or #4 (1/2") rebar for a driveway or patio?
faqs.answer: Use #3 (3/8-inch) rebar on 18-inch or 24-inch centers for 4-inch backyard patios and walkways. Upgrade to #4 (1/2-inch) Grade 60 rebar on 16-inch or 18-inch centers for driveways, garage floors, and slabs over expansive clay soil.

faqs.question: How do you read rebar numbers (#3, #4, #5)?
faqs.answer: US rebar sizes are measured in eighths of an inch. A #3 bar is 3/8 inch in diameter, a #4 bar is 4/8 (1/2) inch in diameter, and a #5 bar is 5/8 inch in diameter.

faqs.question: How much overlap is required when joining two pieces of rebar?
faqs.answer: Standard ACI residential code calls for a lap splice of 30 to 40 times the bar diameter. That equals 15 inches of overlap for #3 (3/8") rebar and 20 inches of overlap for #4 (1/2") rebar. Buying 20-foot bars instead of 10-foot bars cuts splice waste in half.

faqs.question: Is fiberglass rebar as good as steel rebar for flatwork?
faqs.answer: GFRP (pink or green fiberglass rebar) has twice the tensile strength of steel, weighs 75% less (easy to carry in one hand), and never rusts in salted driveways. However, it cannot be bent on site and requires slightly closer chair spacing because it is more flexible.

faqs.question: How many rebar chairs do I need per 100 square feet?
faqs.answer: Place one plastic rebar chair (or concrete brick dobie) every 3 to 4 feet in both directions—roughly 8 to 10 chairs per 100 square feet—so the grid does not sag under the boots of the concrete crew during the pour.

inputs.tooltip: Synthetic underlayment rolls cover 10 squares (1,000 sq ft); #15 felt covers 400 sq ft.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Roof Squares & Shingle Bundles by Footprint & Pitch (Includes 10% Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Roof Area = Footprint × √(1 + (Rise ÷ 12)²); Squares = (Roof Area × (1 + Waste%)) ÷ 100; Bundles = ceil(Squares × 3)
steps: Measure your home’s ground footprint Length × Width (remember to add 1 to 2 feet on each side for roof eave and rake overhangs).
Multiply the flat footprint by the Pitch Multiplier: √(1 + (Rise ÷ 12)²)—for example, 1.118 for a 6/12 roof.
Add 10% waste for a gable roof (or 15% for a hip roof with valleys).
Divide the total square footage by 100 to convert into Roofing Squares (1 square = 100 sq ft).
Multiply Roofing Squares by 3 and round UP to get total shingle bundles.

workedExample.title: Re-Roofing a 2,000 sq ft Footprint Home with a 6/12 Pitch
workedExample.scenario: Your house footprint (including 1-ft eaves) is 50 ft × 40 ft (2,000 sq ft) with a 6/12 gable roof and 10% waste.
steps: Flat Footprint = 50 × 40 = 2,000 sq ft.
Sloped Roof Area (6/12 factor 1.118) = 2,000 × 1.118 = 2,236 sq ft.
Roofing Squares = 2,460 ÷ 100 = 24.60 squares.
Shingle Bundles = ceil(24.60 × 3) = 74 bundles.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 74 bundles of architectural shingles, 3 rolls of 1,000 sq ft synthetic underlayment, 20 pieces of 10-ft drip edge, and 3 bundles of ridge cap.

tipsAndMistakes: Never forget eave and rake overhangs when measuring from the ground: a 16-inch soffit overhang all the way around a 40×50 ft house adds nearly 250 sq ft (2.5 squares / 8 bundles) to your roof!
Install peel-and-stick Ice & Water Shield along the bottom 3 to 6 feet of all eaves (required by IRC code in northern states where January averages ≤ 25°F) and in every valley.
Order dedicada starter strip rolls and pre-cut hip/ridge cap bundles—cutting up expensive architectural laminate shingles for starter courses wastes time and creates bumpy eave edges.

Follow the drip-edge lapping rule: on the bottom EAVES, metal drip edge goes UNDER the underlayment; on the sloped gable RAKES, drip edge goes ON TOP of the underlayment so wind cannot blow rain underneath.
Drive 4 nails per shingle (or 6 nails per shingle in high-wind / coastal zones) right through the reinforced nailing strip—high-nailing above the line voids wind warranties.
Have the supplier boom-truck load the shingle pallets directly onto the roof ridge (or driveway) so you don’t carry 74 bundles (5,200+ lbs) up a ladder.

faqs.question: How many bundles of shingles are in a roofing square?
faqs.answer: One roofing square equals 100 square feet of roof surface. For 95% of standard 3-tab and architectural dimensional asphalt shingles, 3 bundles cover 1 square (33.3 sq ft per bundle). Heavyweight luxury/designer shingles sometimes require 4 or 5 bundles per square.

faqs.question: How much does a bundle of architectural shingles weigh?
faqs.answer: A single bundle of architectural asphalt shingles weighs between 65 and 80 pounds (195 to 240 pounds per roofing square). A 25-square roof weighs roughly 5,000 to 6,000 pounds.

faqs.question: Should I tear off old shingles or roof over them?
faqs.answer: While building codes often allow a maximum of two shingle layers if the deck is flat, tearing off down to bare wood sheathing is strongly recommended. A tear-off lets you inspect and replace rotted OSB decking, install fresh ice-and-water shield, and ensures your new shingles lay flat and qualify for full manufacturer warranties.

faqs.question: Why does a hip roof need 15% waste instead of 10%?
faqs.answer: A hip roof slopes on all four sides, meaning every course ends in a 45-degree diagonal cut at four hip ridges (plus any intersecting valleys). Those diagonal off-cuts cannot all be flipped and reused, adding ~5% more scrap than a straight gable roof.

faqs.question: How many linear feet does 1 bundle of ridge cap shingles cover?
faqs.answer: One bundle of standard hip and ridge cap shingles (at a 5-inch to 5.5-inch exposure) covers approximately 25 to 33 linear feet of roof ridge.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Roof Pitch Conversion Table (X/12 to Degrees, Grade % & Area Multiplier)

howToCalculate.formula: Pitch (X/12) = (Rise ÷ Run) × 12; Angle (°) = arctan(Rise ÷ Run) × (180 ÷ π); Multiplier = √(1 + (Pitch ÷ 12)²)
steps: Hold a 12-inch level horizontally against the underside of a rafter (or top of the roof) and measure vertically from the end of the level to the roof surface to find the Rise.
If you measured over a different horizontal run, normalize to 12 inches: Pitch = (Rise ÷ Run) × 12.
Find the roof angle in degrees using the inverse tangent: Angle = arctan(Rise ÷ Run) × 57.2958.
Find the Roof Area Multiplier using the Pythagorean theorem: √(1 + (Rise ÷ Run)²).

workedExample.title: Calculating Rafter Length & Area Factor for a 6/12 Roof on a 24-ft Wide House
workedExample.scenario: Your roof rises 6 inches for every 12 inches of horizontal run across a 24-ft wide gable house (12-ft half-span).
steps: Pitch = 6/12 (50% grade).
Angle in Degrees = arctan(6 ÷ 12) = 26.57°.
Pitch Area Multiplier = √(1 + (6 ÷ 12)²) = √1.25 = 1.118.
Ridge Height = 12 ft half-span × (6 ÷ 12) = 6.0 ft above top wall plate.
Common Rafter Length = 12 ft × 1.118 = 13.42 ft (plus tail overhang).
workedExample.finalAnswer: A 6/12 roof sits at a 26.6° angle, multiplies flat footprint area by 1.118×, and requires 13.42-ft rafters before overhang.

tipsAndMistakes: Measure inside the attic whenever possible: holding a 12-inch level against a bare wood rafter in the attic avoids climbing onto a slippery roof and avoids errors caused by cupped shingle edges.

Know the minimum legal pitch for your roofing material: standard asphalt shingles require at least a 2/12 pitch (IRC R905.2.2); below 2/12, you must use EPDM rubber, TPO, or modified bitumen roll roofing.
Roofs between 2/12 and 4/12 are "low-slope" and require double-layer underlayment or full peel-and-stick ice/water membrane under asphalt shingles.
Do not forget to add your soffit overhang (rafter tail) when ordering rafter lumber: a 13.42-ft rafter with a 1.5-ft overhang requires a 16-ft 2×8 or 2×10 board.
Use roof jacks and a safety harness on any roof steeper than 7/12 (30.3°).
Solar panel installers typically consider 6/12 to 8/12 (26° to 34°) the sweet spot for year-round US solar output.

faqs.question: What is the difference between roof pitch and roof slope?
faqs.answer: In everyday contractor terminology, "pitch" and "slope" both refer to rise over 12 inches of run (e.g., 6/12). Historically in classic framing carpentry, "pitch" meant total rise divided by total building span (so a 6/12 slope was called a "1/4 pitch"), which is why modern plans always write X/12 to avoid confusion.

faqs.question: What roof pitch is a 45-degree angle?
faqs.answer: A 12/12 roof pitch (12 inches of vertical rise for every 12 inches of horizontal run) equals an exact 45-degree angle (100% slope grade) and has a 1.414× surface area multiplier.

faqs.question: What is the steepest roof pitch you can walk on without roof jacks?
faqs.answer: Most experienced roofers consider 6/12 (26.6°) to 7/12 (30.3°) the upper limit for walking in soft-rubber roofing boots on dry asphalt shingles. At 8/12 (33.7°) and steeper, OSHA-compliant roof jacks, toe boards, and fall-arrest harnesses are essential.

faqs.question: What is the best roof pitch for heavy snow sheds?
faqs.answer: In northern snow-belt states, pitches of 8/12 to 12/12 (especially with standing-seam metal roofing) shed heavy snow loads naturally and minimize ice-dam pooling along the eaves.

faqs.question: How do I set my circular saw bevel for plumb and seat cuts?
faqs.answer: Your rafter plumb cut angle at the ridge equals the roof angle in degrees (e.g., 26.5° for a 6/12 roof), while the horizontal birdsmouth seat cut is its complement (90° − 26.5° = 63.5°). You can also mark both directly with a Swanson Speed Square.
