Add 10% for section overlaps and divide by 10 to find how many 10-ft K-style gutter sections you need.
Divide total eave length by 35 feet (and ensure at least 1 downspout per separate run) to find the number of downspout drops.
Multiply each downspout by 3 elbows (2 at the soffit offset + 1 at the bottom kick-out) and 1 drop outlet.
Divide eave length in inches by 24 inches (or 16 inches in snow zones) to get the number of screw-in hidden hangers.

workedExample.title: Installing Gutters on a 120-Ft Eave Single-Story Home (3 Runs)
workedExample.scenario: Your 1-story home (10-ft eaves) has 120 linear feet of eaves across 3 separate straight runs.
steps: Gutter Length w/ 10% waste = 120 × 1.10 = 132 ft → ceil(132 ÷ 10) = 14 sections.
Downspout Locations = max(3 runs, ceil(120 ÷ 35)) = 4 downspouts.
Downspout 10-Ft Pipes = (4 × 10 ft) ÷ 10 = 4 pipes.
Hidden Hangers @ 24" OC = ceil((120 × 12) ÷ 24) + 3 = 63 hangers.
Fittings = 6 end caps (2 per run), 12 elbows (3 per downspout), and 4 drop outlets.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Buy 14 gutter sections (10-ft), 4 downspout pipes (10-ft), 63 hidden hangers, 12 elbows, 6 end caps, and 4 drop outlets.

tipsAndMistakes: Slope every gutter run 1/4 inch (or at least 1/8 inch) downward for every 10 feet toward the downspout: a dead-level gutter holds standing water that breeds mosquitoes and rots fascia boards.
For gutter runs longer than 40 feet, pitch the center high and put a downspout at BOTH ends so each half only slopes 20 feet.
Mount gutters so the back lip tucks UNDER the metal roof drip edge—otherwise water wicks behind the gutter and rots your wood fascia.
Use hidden screw-in fascia hangers rather than old-fashioned spike-and-ferrule nails, which back out of wood after a few freeze-thaw winters.
Upgrade from 2×3" downspouts to 3×4" oversized downspouts if you have trees overhead: a 3×4" downspout has double the opening area and rarely clogs with oak leaves.
Extend downspout discharge at least 4 to 6 feet away from your foundation sill to prevent basement seepage.

faqs.question: When should I upgrade from 5-inch to 6-inch gutters?
faqs.answer: Standard 5-inch K-style gutters with 2×3" downspouts handle most single-story roofs up to 1,500 sq ft of drainage area. Upgrade to 6-inch K-style gutters with 3×4" downspouts if you have a large two-story roof, a steep pitch (8/12+), or a slick metal/tile roof where water shoots fast during downpours.

faqs.question: How far apart should gutter hangers be spaced?
faqs.answer: In mild and moderate climates, space hidden screw-in gutter hangers every 24 inches on center into solid 1×6 fascia or rafter tails. In northern snow-belt states where heavy ice slides off the roof, space hangers every 16 to 18 inches on center.

faqs.question: What is the difference between A-style and B-style downspout elbows?
faqs.answer: An A-elbow bends forward and backward (used at the top soffit offset to bring the downspout back from the eave to the house wall and at the bottom kick-out). A B-elbow bends left or right sideways along the wall when routing a downspout around a corner.

faqs.question: Are seamless gutters better than DIY 10-ft sectional gutters?
faqs.answer: Professional roll-formed seamless aluminum gutters have joints only at corners and downspouts, eliminating mid-run leak points. However, DIY 10-foot aluminum or vinyl sectional gutters cost 60% less and won’t leak if you rivet the lap joints and seal them with tripolymer gutter sealant.

faqs.question: How many square feet of roof can one downspout drain?
faqs.answer: One standard 2×3-inch downspout drains approximately 600 square feet of roof watershed area. One oversized 3×4-inch downspout drains up to 1,200 square feet of roof area.

inputs.label: Gable Angle & Lap Waste %

inputs.name: pricePerSquare

quickReferenceMeta.title: Siding Squares Needed by Home Size (Includes Gables & 10% Waste)

howToCalculate.formula: Net Wall Area = (Perimeter × Height) + (Gables × 0.5 × Width × Height) − Openings; Siding Squares = ceil((Net Area × (1 + Waste%)) ÷ 100)
steps: Multiply your House Perimeter by the Wall Height (from foundation sill to soffit eave) to get main wall square footage.
Add triangular gable wall areas: Number of Gables × 0.5 × Gable Width × Gable Height.
Subtract 21 sq ft per entry door, 15 sq ft per window, and 112 sq ft per 2-car garage door.
Multiply by 1.10 to add 10% cutting and lap waste (angled gable cuts generate extra scrap).
Divide total square footage by 100 to convert into Siding Squares (1 square = 100 sq ft).

workedExample.title: Siding a 160-Ft Perimeter Ranch Home with 2 Gables
workedExample.scenario: A single-story home has a 160-ft perimeter, 10-ft walls, 2 gables (26×7 ft), 2 doors, 10 windows, and 1 garage door.
steps: Main Walls = 160 × 10 = 1,600 sq ft; Gables = 2 × (0.5 × 26 × 7) = 182 sq ft.
Gross Area = 1,782 sq ft.
Openings = (2 × 21) + (10 × 15) + 112 = 304 sq ft. Net Area = 1,478 sq ft.
Siding Squares = 1,625.8 ÷ 100 = 16.26 → Order 17 squares.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 17 squares of siding, 4 outside corner posts (10-ft), 23 pieces of J-channel (12.5-ft), and 3 rolls of housewrap.

tipsAndMistakes: Never nail vinyl siding tight! Leave a 1/32-inch (credit-card thickness) gap between the roofing nail head and the vinyl nailing hem, and center the nail in the slot—A 12-foot vinyl panel expands and contracts by up to 1/2 inch between winter and summer and will buckle if pinned tight.
Leave a 1/4-inch clearance gap inside all J-channels and corner posts (3/8 inch if installing in freezing weather below 40°F) to allow horizontal thermal expansion.
Overlap horizontal vinyl panels by 1 to 1.25 inches, and stagger butt seams by at least 3 feet so seams never stack vertically, facing the overlap away from the street.
For James Hardie fiber-cement lap siding, prime or factory-seal all field-cut ends and install flashing strips ("bearings/joint flashings") behind every butt joint.
Always tape housewrap seams with official contractor seam tape and flash window sills/jambs in shingle-fashion (bottom sill first, jambs second, top head flashing last).
Snap a dead-level chalk line around the entire house from the lowest corner before nailing your bottom starter strip.

faqs.question: How many square feet are in a square of siding?
faqs.answer: One "square" of exterior siding covers exactly 100 square feet of installed wall area. Vinyl siding is typically packaged with 2 squares (200 sq ft) per carton, or 1 square (100 sq ft) per carton for thicker insulated or shake profiles.

faqs.question: Should I deduct windows and doors when ordering vinyl siding?
faqs.answer: Our calculator deducts standard openings and adds 10% waste for accuracy. Many pros use a quick field rule: deduct large garage doors and picture windows, but leave small 3×4 windows in the gross calculation to automatically cover gable angle waste.

faqs.question: How much J-channel and starter strip do I need?
faqs.answer: You need metal or vinyl starter strip along the entire bottom perimeter of the house (minus doorways). You need J-channel around the top and sides of every window and door, along roof gable rakes, and where siding meets soffits.

faqs.question: Vinyl vs. Fiber-Cement (HardiePlank) siding: which is better?
faqs.answer: Vinyl siding is lightweight, never needs painting, and costs roughly half as much to install, though it can crack in severe hail or warp near hot BBQ grills. Fiber-cement (made of Portland cement, sand, and cellulose) is fire-resistant, woodpecker-proof, and looks like real painted cedar.

faqs.question: How many nails do I need per square of vinyl siding?
faqs.answer: Nailing into studs every 16 inches on center requires roughly 110 to 130 corrosion-resistant galvanized or aluminum roofing nails (1.5" to 2" long) per square—about 1.5 to 2 pounds of nails per square.

How to remember the 3-inch rule of thumb: 1 cubic yard of mulch covers roughly 100 square feet at 3 inches deep (108 sq ft exact).

Don’t over-mulch existing beds: if you still have 1.5 inches of old mulch from last year, you only need a 1-to-1.5-inch top-off to reach 3 inches total—matting 5+ inches of mulch suffocates plant roots.
Apply a granular pre-emergent weed preventer (like Preen / corn gluten) and water it in BEFORE spreading fresh mulch.
Cut a crisp 3-inch-deep V-trench ("spade edge") along the lawn border with a flat edging spade so rain doesn’t float mulch into your grass.
Wait 24 hours of dry sun after spreading color-enhanced (black, brown, or red) dyed mulch before running sprinklers so the iron-oxide or carbon dye sets permanently.

faqs.question: How many 2 cu ft bags of mulch equal 1 cubic yard?
faqs.answer: One cubic yard contains 27 cubic feet. Divided by 2 cubic feet per standard bag, it takes exactly 13.5 bags (buy 14 bags) of mulch to equal 1 cubic yard. If using smaller 1.5 cu ft bags, it takes 18 bags per cubic yard.

faqs.question: How much area does 1 cubic yard of mulch cover?
faqs.answer: One cubic yard (27 cu ft) covers 324 square feet at 1 inch deep, 162 square feet at 2 inches deep, 108 square feet at 3 inches deep, and 81 square feet at 4 inches deep.

faqs.question: Is it cheaper to buy bagged mulch or bulk delivery?
faqs.answer: For fewer than 25 to 30 bags (about 2 cubic yards), buying 2 cu ft bags on spring promo sales ($2.50–$3.50/bag) is usually cheaper because bulk landscape yards charge a $50–$95 dump-truck delivery fee. Above 3 cubic yards (40+ bags), bulk delivery saves money and eliminates hauling plastic bags.

faqs.question: How much does a 2 cu ft bag or cubic yard of mulch weigh?
faqs.answer: A dry 2 cu ft bag of cedar or pine bark weighs 20 to 30 pounds, while a damp bag of triple-shredded hardwood weighs 35 to 45 pounds. One bulk cubic yard of hardwood mulch weighs roughly 600 to 800 pounds.

faqs.question: Should I put plastic or landscape fabric under wood mulch?
faqs.answer: Avoid black plastic (which blocks water and oxygen) and skip fabric under organic wood mulch in perennial flower beds. Over 1 to 2 years, wood mulch decomposes into rich humus on top of the fabric, and weed seeds blow in and root right into the fabric anyway. Instead, use 3 inches of mulch directly over soil (or a single layer of brown kraft cardboard).

Build new driveways in layers: lay 3–4" of large #3 stone (1.5–2" fist-sized rock) at the bottom for structure, topped with 2–3" of #57 or crusher-run.
Grade a 2% center crown (about 2 inches higher down the middle of a 12-foot driveway than the edges) so rain sheets off into side ditches instead of carving ruts down the wheel tracks.
Ask the dump-truck driver to "tailgate spread" your stone! A skilled driver can chain the tailgate to a 4-inch gap and dump while rolling forward, saving you 6 hours of shoveling.
Keep your payload limits in mind: a standard half-ton pickup truck bed safely carries only 0.5 to 0.75 tons (about half a scoop) of gravel.

faqs.question: How many tons are in 1 cubic yard of gravel?
faqs.answer: One cubic yard (27 cubic feet) of standard crushed stone or limestone weighs approximately 1.4 tons (2,800 pounds). Pea gravel weighs ~1.35 tons (2,700 lbs) per cubic yard, while crusher-run with dense stone dust weighs ~1.45 to 1.50 tons (2,900–3,000 lbs) per cubic yard.

faqs.question: How much area does 1 ton of gravel cover?
faqs.answer: One ton of gravel equals roughly 19.3 cubic feet (0.71 cubic yards). It covers about 115 square feet at 2 inches deep, 77 square feet at 3 inches deep, or 58 square feet at 4 inches deep.

faqs.question: What is #57 stone vs. crusher run (#411)?
faqs.answer: #57 stone is washed, angular crushed rock (roughly 1/2" to 1" golf-ball size) with all fine dust screened out—ideal for top-dressing driveways, French drains, and concrete pads. Crusher run (also called QP, DGA, or #411) blends angular stone with powdered stone dust that packs into a solid, concrete-like crust when dampened and tamped.

faqs.question: How many 50-lb bags of gravel equal 1 ton or 1 cubic yard?
faqs.answer: One ton (2,000 lbs) equals 40 bags of 50-lb gravel. One cubic yard (~2,800 lbs) equals 54 to 56 bags of 50-lb (0.5 cu ft) gravel—which is why bulk quarry delivery is 70% cheaper for anything over 1 ton.

faqs.question: How many tons can a single dump truck deliver?
faqs.answer: A small single-axle landscape dump truck carries 5 to 7 tons, a standard tandem-axle dump truck carries 14 to 16 tons, and a tri-axle dump truck carries 20 to 24 tons.

Add 10% for watering and roller settling, then divide by 27 to get Cubic Yards.

tipsAndMistakes: Know the difference between "Fill Dirt" and "Screened Topsoil": fill dirt is rocky subsoil with zero organic matter used only for deep hole backfilling; always order "pulverized screened topsoil" (or a 50/50 topsoil-compost "garden blend") for lawns and plants.
Don’t fill a raised vegetable bed with 100% heavy topsoil! Pure clay-loam topsoil compacts into a brick in raised beds; use a 50% screened topsoil + 30% compost + 20% coarse sand/perlite mix.

Rototill 1 inch of new topsoil into the top 2 inches of your existing native soil before spreading the rest—dumping new loam flat on top of slick hardpan clay creates a "perched water table" interface that roots won’t cross.
Use a water-filled lawn roller (filled only 1/3 full) after raking new lawn soil so footprints don’t sink when seeding or laying sod.

For deep 24-inch raised beds, save 40% on soil using the "Hugelkultur" method: fill the bottom 8 inches with untreated hardwood logs, branches, and shredded leaves before topping with 16 inches of garden soil.
Cover bulk topsoil piles with a tarp if rain is forecast before you finish wheelbarrowing—wet soil weighs 35% more!

faqs.question: How many 40-lb bags of topsoil are in a cubic yard?
faqs.answer: A standard 40-pound bag of topsoil holds 0.75 cubic feet. Because 1 cubic yard equals 27 cubic feet, it takes exactly 36 bags (27 ÷ 0.75 = 36) of 40-lb topsoil to equal 1 cubic yard.

faqs.question: How much does 1 cubic yard of topsoil weigh?
faqs.answer: Dry, screened pulverized topsoil weighs roughly 2,000 to 2,200 pounds (1.0 to 1.1 tons) per cubic yard. If the soil is wet from rain, weight jumps to 2,600 to 3,000 pounds (1.3 to 1.5 tons) per cubic yard.

faqs.question: How deep should topsoil be for grass seed or sod?
faqs.answer: Turfgrass roots need 4 to 6 inches of loose, nutrient-rich topsoil to survive summer drought. If topdressing an existing thin lawn before overseeding, spread a 1/4-inch to 1/2-inch layer of screened compost/topsoil with a leveling rake so existing grass blades aren’t smothered.

faqs.question: How much soil does one 4×8 raised garden bed hold?
faqs.answer: A 4×8 ft bed that is 10 inches deep holds 26.7 cubic feet—almost exactly 1 cubic yard. A 4×8 ft bed that is 12 inches deep holds 32 cubic feet (1.19 cubic yards).

faqs.question: What is the difference between topsoil, garden soil, and potting mix?
faqs.answer: Topsoil is screened natural mineral earth used for grading lawns. Garden soil is topsoil amended with bark fines and compost for in-ground flower beds. Potting mix contains zero actual dirt—it is a lightweight blend of peat moss, coco coir, perlite, and bark designed for containers.

tipsAndMistakes: Lay sod on the SAME DAY it is delivered! Rolled-up sod on a pallet generates intense biological compost heat inside the stack and will turn yellow and cook to death within 24 to 36 hours in warm weather.
Grade your soil 1 inch BELOW sidewalks and driveways before laying sod so the 1-inch-thick root mat sits flush with the concrete.
Start laying your first row along the longest straight edge (like a driveway or patio), and stagger end seams in a running brick pattern so water cannot erode channels down continuous seams.
Butt edges tightly together without overlapping, and use a serrated bread knife or linoleum hook knife to trim cleanly around curved beds and sprinkler heads.
Roll the finished lawn with a 1/3-full water roller to press roots firmly against the damp soil and eliminate air pockets that dry out root hairs.
Water immediately: lift a corner of a roll after watering—the soil underneath should be soggy 3 inches down for the first 10 to 14 days until roots knit firmly.

faqs.question: How many square feet are on a pallet of sod?
faqs.answer: A standard pallet of sod covers 450 square feet in most northern and transition-zone markets (45 rolls at 10 sq ft each, or 50 rolls at 9 sq ft each). In southern markets (Florida, Texas, Georgia), Bermuda, Zoysia, and St. Augustine pallets typically cover 450 to 500 square feet.

faqs.question: How much does a pallet or roll of sod weigh?
faqs.answer: A single 10-square-foot roll of freshly harvested sod weighs 30 to 40 pounds depending on soil moisture. A full 450-square-foot pallet weighs between 1,500 and 2,500 pounds—requiring a forklift for delivery and a wheelbarrow for moving rolls to the backyard.

faqs.question: Can I lay new sod right over existing dead grass?
faqs.answer: No! Laying sod over old grass or weeds creates a thatch barrier that stops roots from reaching the soil and allows old weeds to punch right through. Rent a motorized sod cutter to slice off the old turf, rototill 2 inches of compost/topsoil into the dirt, and rake smooth.

faqs.question: When can I mow and walk on new sod?
faqs.answer: Keep heavy foot traffic and pets off new sod for the first 14 days while the soil is kept soft and wet. Perform the "tug test" after 10–14 days: if you tug on the grass blades and the roll resists lifting because white roots have anchored into the dirt, let the soil firm up for a day and mow on the highest deck setting.

faqs.question: Should I fertilize under new sod?
faqs.answer: Yes—apply a high-phosphorus "Starter Fertilizer" (such as 18-24-12 or 24-25-4) directly to the prepared soil right before unrolling the sod so phosphorus is immediately available at the root zone.

workedExample.scenario: You have 5,000 sq ft of bare prepared topsoil and are planting Turf-Type Tall Fescue at 8 lbs per 1,000 sq ft.

tipsAndMistakes: Why Bluegrass uses 3 lbs/1,000 sq ft while Tall Fescue uses 8 lbs: it’s all about seed size! One pound of Kentucky Bluegrass contains ~2.1 million tiny seeds, whereas one pound of Tall Fescue contains only ~225,000 large seeds.

More seed is NOT better: dumping double the recommended seed rate forces millions of seedlings to compete for the same square inch of water and sunlight, resulting in weak, spindly turf that dies from "damping-off" fungus.
Check the seed analysis tag on the back of the bag: look for "0.00% Weed Seed" and "0.00% Other Crop Seed" (which is often coarse pasture orchardgrass that forms ugly lime-green clumps).

Beware of "coated" seed math: many big-box brands coat their seed in 50% water-absorbent clay/polymer weight—meaning a 20-lb bag only contains 10 lbs of actual grass seed! Increase your rate if buying 50%-coated seed.
Divide your seed into two halves and walk your broadcast spreader at half-rate North-to-South, then the second half East-to-West in a crisscross grid so you never leave striped bare misses.
Seed-to-soil contact is everything: aerate or power-rake before overseeding, and lightly roll or rake seed 1/8" into the soil.

faqs.question: When is the best month to plant grass seed?
faqs.answer: For cool-season grasses (Tall Fescue, Kentucky Bluegrass, Ryegrass) in the northern two-thirds of the US, late summer to early fall (August 15 – October 1) is by far the best window because soil is warm, weeds are dying, and autumn rains aid germination. For warm-season grasses (Bermuda, Zoysia), plant in late spring once soil hits 65°F+.

faqs.question: How often should I water new grass seed?
faqs.answer: Do not deep-water once a day! New grass seeds sit in the top 1/4 inch of soil and die if they dry out once after swelling. Mist lightly for 5 to 10 minutes 2 to 3 times per day (morning, noon, and 4 PM) to keep the top 1/2 inch of soil constantly damp until grass reaches 2 inches tall.

faqs.question: How long does grass seed take to germinate?
faqs.answer: Perennial Ryegrass sprouts fastest in 5 to 10 days; Turf-Type Tall Fescue and Fine Fescue sprout in 7 to 14 days; Bermuda takes 10 to 21 days; and Kentucky Bluegrass takes the longest at 14 to 28 days.

faqs.question: Can I apply Crabgrass Preventer (weed & feed) when seeding?
faqs.answer: Never apply standard pre-emergent crabgrass preventer (prodiamine or dithiopyr) when seeding—it blocks grass seed from germinating for 3 months! The only herbicide safe to apply at seeding time is Mesotrione (Tenacity / Scotts Starter Food + Weed Preventer).

faqs.question: Should I cover bare grass seed with straw or peat moss?
faqs.answer: Yes—a thin layer of clean wheat straw (where you can still see 50% of the dirt through the straw) or 1/8 inch of peat moss holds moisture, stops birds from eating the seed, and prevents heavy rain from washing seed into puddles.

Use 3 horizontal 2×4 rails on any 6-foot fence: trying to save $150 by using only 2 rails allows sun-baked pickets to cup and warp wildly in the middle.

Butt wet pressure-treated pickets tightly together with zero gap: fresh green-treated pine shrinks by 1/8" to 1/4" in width as it dries over the first 60 days, naturally creating a small breathing gap. (For kiln-dried cedar, leave a framing-nail thickness gap so rain expansion doesn’t buckle them).
Slope the top of each concrete post footing slightly like a dome above dirt level so rainwater sheds away from the wood post base.

Brace every gate frame with a diagonal compression 2×4 running from the bottom hinge corner UP to the top latch corner (or use a steel anti-sag cable kit)—a diagonal running the opposite way stretches in tension and lets the gate drag on the ground.

faqs.question: How many pickets do I need for 100 feet of privacy fence?
faqs.answer: Using standard 1×6 pickets (which actually measure 5.5 inches wide) butted edge-to-edge with zero gap, 100 linear feet (1,200 inches) requires 219 net pickets. Adding 10% to cull warped or split boards at the store brings your order to 240 pickets.

faqs.question: How many bags of concrete do I need per fence post?
faqs.answer: For a standard 10-inch diameter hole dug 30 inches deep with a 4×4 post, you need roughly 1.1 cubic feet of concrete—which equals two 80-lb bags (0.60 cu ft each) or three 50-lb bags of fast-setting red-bag concrete (0.375 cu ft each).

faqs.question: Should I use nails or screws to attach fence pickets?
faqs.answer: Hot-dipped galvanized or stainless-steel 1-3/4" ring-shank siding nails fired from a coil nailer are fastest, while #8 × 1-5/8" coated exterior star-drive deck screws make it easy to unscrew and swap out a warped picket later. Never use electro-galvanized indoor nails, which bleed black rust streaks down cedar and pine.

faqs.question: How deep should fence posts be buried?
faqs.answer: Follow the 1/3 rule: bury at least one-third of the total post length underground (2 feet deep for a 4-ft fence; 2.5 to 3 feet deep for a 6-ft fence). In northern cold climates, dig corner and gate posts below the local frost line (36–48 inches) so frost heave doesn’t jam the gate latch.

faqs.question: Which side of a wood fence faces the neighbor ("good neighbor" rule)?
faqs.answer: Nearly all municipal zoning codes and HOA rules require the smooth finished picket side ("good side") to face outward toward neighbors and the street, with the posts and 2×4 rails facing inward toward your own yard.

Multiply Rows × Boards per Row × 1.10 (for 10% waste) and round up.
Find Floor Joists: divide Deck Length (in inches) by 16" (or 12") on-center, add 1 end joist, and add 2 boards for the house ledger and front rim joist.
Multiply total deck square footage by 3.5 to estimate deck screws or hidden clips.

workedExample.title: Framing & Decking a 12×16 ft Backyard Deck
workedExample.scenario: You are building a 16 ft long × 12 ft wide deck using 16-ft 5/4×6 boards (5.5" wide, 1/8" gap) on joists spaced 16" on-center.
steps: Boards per Row = 16 ft ÷ 16 ft = 1 board per row.
Total Deck Boards w/ 10% waste = ceil(25.6 × 1 × 1.10) = 29 boards (16-ft).
Interior Joists @ 16" OC = ceil((16 × 12) ÷ 16) + 1 = 13 joists + 2 rim/ledger = 15 framing boards.
Fasteners = ceil(192 sq ft × 3.5 × 1.05) = 706 screws.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 29 deck boards (16-ft), 15 floor joists, 13 joist hangers, and two 350-count buckets of exterior deck screws.

tipsAndMistakes: Space joists 12 inches on-center (instead of 16 inches) if you are installing composite/PVC decking—especially in hot southern sun or at a 45-degree angle—so the synthetic boards never feel bouncy underfoot.
Crown every wood floor joist upward: sight down the narrow edge of each 2×8 or 2×10 board and place the slight natural hump ("crown") facing UP so gravity flattens the floor under load.

Apply butyl joist tape over the top edge of all wood joists and double beams before laying expensive composite decking—butyl tape seals around deck screws and stops joists from rotting after 10 years.

Never attach a deck ledger board over vinyl or wood siding! Cut the siding out, slide metal Z-flashing under the housewrap and over the ledger, and fasten the ledger directly to the house rim joist with 1/2" lag screws or structural ledger locks (IRC R507.9).
Let the ends of your deck boards run 1 to 2 inches wild past the side rim joists as you screw them down, then snap a chalk line and make one single straight pass with a circular saw at the end.

Use only hot-dipped galvanized (G185) or stainless steel joist hangers and structural connector screws (never drywall or regular deck screws in joist hangers!) because ACQ copper preservative corrodes thin zinc.

faqs.question: How many 5/4×6 deck boards do I need per foot of deck width?
faqs.answer: Because a nominal 5/4×6 (or 2×6) board actually measures 5.5 inches wide (plus a 1/8" gap = 5.625 inches), it takes 2.13 rows of boards for every 1 foot of deck width—or roughly 26 rows for a 12-foot-wide deck.

faqs.question: What size floor joists do I need for a 12-foot deck span?
faqs.answer: Under IRC Table R507.6 (Southern Pine #2 at 16" on-center), 2×8 joists span up to 11 ft 10 in, 2×10 joists span up to 14 ft 0 in, and 2×12 joists span up to 16 ft 6 in (plus up to a 2-foot cantilever overhang beyond a dropped beam).

faqs.question: How many deck screws do I need per 100 square feet?
faqs.answer: Driving two 2-1/2" star-drive deck screws at every 16-inch joist crossing uses roughly 350 screws (one 5-lb tub) per 100 square feet of 5/4×6 decking. If joists are spaced 12 inches on-center, plan on 450 screws per 100 square feet.

faqs.question: Should wood deck boards be installed bark-side up or bark-side down?
faqs.answer: Look at the curved growth rings on the cut end of the board. The Timber Decking and Cladding Association and modern mill specs recommend laying flatsawn boards so the outer growth rings point UP ("smile down / frown up" = bark side up), which sheds water better and minimizes splintering.

faqs.question: Can I build a deck longer than 16 or 20 feet without ugly butt joints?
faqs.answer: Yes! Install a double joist down the center of the deck and run a single perpendicular "breaker board" (divider board) down the middle between the two double joists. Two 12-foot or 16-foot sections meet cleanly against the breaker board with zero end-to-end butt joints.

howToCalculate.formula: Net Area = (2 × (L + W) × H) + (L × W Ceiling) − Openings; Sheets = ceil((Net Area × (1 + Waste%)) ÷ 32)
steps: Calculate Gross Wall Area: 2 × (Room Length + Room Width) × Wall Height.
If hanging ceiling drywall, add Length × Width.
Subtract 21 sq ft per doorway and 15 sq ft per window to get Net Drywall Area.
Add 10% waste and divide by 32 sq ft (for 4×8 sheets) or 48 sq ft (for 4×12 sheets), then round up.
Multiply Net Area ÷ 100 × 1.4 gallons for Joint Compound, Net Area × 0.37 for Joint Tape (ft), and Sheets × 32 for Screws.

workedExample.title: Drywalling a 12×12 ft Bedroom (Walls + 8-Ft Ceiling)
workedExample.scenario: You are hanging 4×8 drywall on the walls and ceiling of a 12 ft × 12 ft room (8-ft high) with 2 doors and 2 windows.
steps: Wall Area = 2 × (12 + 12) × 8 = 384 sq ft; Ceiling = 12 × 12 = 144 sq ft.
Gross Area = 528 sq ft − 72 sq ft openings = 456 net sq ft.
With 10% waste = 456 × 1.10 = 501.6 sq ft.
4×8 Sheets = ceil(501.6 ÷ 32) = 16 sheets.
Mud = 4.56 × 1.4 = 6.4 gal (two 4.5-gal buckets); Tape = 169 ft (1 roll); Screws = 16 × 32 = 512 screws.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Order 16 sheets of 4×8 drywall, two 4.5-gallon buckets of joint compound, 1 roll of 250-ft paper tape, and one 5-lb box of 1-1/4" screws.

tipsAndMistakes: Always hang the CEILING drywall first before the walls! That way, the top edge of the wall panels pushes up tightly against the perimeter of the ceiling panels to support the corners.

Hang wall sheets HORIZONTALLY (perpendicular to the studs) rather than vertically: horizontal sheets bridge across more studs for rigid walls, and put the single tapered seam at comfortable waist height (4 feet off the floor) for easy mudding.

Stagger vertical butt joints between top and bottom rows so four sheet corners never meet in a cross ("railroad tracks"), and never place a vertical seam directly aligned with the side of a door or window frame (where door slamming will crack the joint).

Use a $10 dimpler bit on your drill: drywall screws must sit in a 1/32-inch dimple WITHOUT tearing through the face paper—once the screw head rips through the brown paper, it has zero holding power in crumbly gypsum.

Use creased paper tape (not fiberglass mesh tape) with ready-mixed bucket compound for all inside corners and flat joints; mesh tape only reaches full strength when embedded in fast-setting hot mud (Durabond/Easy Sand).
Lift bottom wall sheets 1/2 inch off the subfloor with a foot drywall lifter so moisture on the floor never wicks into the gypsum.

faqs.question: How many square feet does one sheet of drywall cover?
faqs.answer: A standard 4×8-foot drywall sheet covers 32 square feet. A 4×10-foot sheet covers 40 square feet, and a 4×12-foot sheet covers 48 square feet.

faqs.question: Should I use 1/2-inch or 5/8-inch drywall?
faqs.answer: Use 1/2-inch ultralight drywall for standard residential walls and ceilings with joists spaced 16 inches on-center. Upgrade to 5/8-inch drywall on ceilings framed 24 inches on-center (to prevent sagging), on shared bedroom walls for soundproofing, and wherever building code requires 5/8" Type X fire-rated board (such as attached garage walls and ceilings).

faqs.question: How many screws do I need per 4×8 sheet of drywall?
faqs.answer: Per the USG Sheetrock Construction Handbook, residential walls framed 16 inches on-center require roughly 32 screws per 4×8 sheet (spaced every 16" in the field and 8" along seams). Ceilings require 36 to 40 screws per 4×8 sheet (spaced every 12" in the field).

faqs.question: How much joint compound (mud) do I need per sheet of drywall?
faqs.answer: Three coats of taping and finishing consume roughly 0.45 gallons (about 5.5 lbs) of ready-mixed joint compound per 4×8 sheet—meaning one 4.5-gallon bucket finishes 9 to 10 sheets (about 300 to 320 square feet).

faqs.question: What size drywall screws should I buy?
faqs.answer: For 1/2-inch drywall attached to wood studs, use #6 × 1-1/4 inch coarse-thread bugle-head phosphate drywall screws. For 5/8-inch Type X drywall on wood studs, use 1-5/8 inch coarse-thread screws. For metal studs, use fine-thread self-tapping screws.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Stair Risers, Treads & Stringer Lengths for Common Floor Heights

howToCalculate.formula: Risers = ceil(Total Rise ÷ 7.75"); Exact Riser = Total Rise ÷ Risers; Treads = Risers − 1; Total Run = Treads × Tread Depth; Stringer = √(Rise² + Run²)
steps: Measure the exact vertical Total Rise in inches from the finished lower floor (or patio pad) to the top of the finished upper floor.
Divide Total Rise by 7.75 inches (the IRC maximum riser height) and round UP to the next whole number to get the Number of Risers.
Divide Total Rise by the Number of Risers to get your Exact Riser Height (every step must be identical within 3/8").
Subtract 1 from Risers to get the Number of Treads (for standard flush-mount stringers where the upper deck acts as the final step).
Multiply Treads × Tread Depth (min 10") to get Total Horizontal Run, and use √(Total Rise² + Total Run²) to find Stringer Length.

workedExample.title: Designing an Interior Staircase for a 108-Inch Total Rise
workedExample.scenario: Your floor-to-floor vertical rise is 108 inches (9 feet), using a 10.5-inch tread depth and 36-inch stair width.
steps: Number of Risers = ceil(108 ÷ 7.75) = ceil(13.94) = 14 risers.
Exact Riser Height = 108 ÷ 14 = 7.71 inches (passes IRC ≤ 7.75" max!).
Number of Treads = 14 − 1 = 13 treads.
Total Horizontal Run = 13 × 10.5" = 136.5 inches (11.38 feet).
Stringer Length = √(108² + 136.5²) = 174.1 inches (14.51 feet → buy 16-ft 2×12 boards).
workedExample.finalAnswer: Cut 3 stringers with 14 risers at 7.71" (~7-11/16") and 13 treads at 10.5" out of 16-ft 2×12 lumber.

tipsAndMistakes: NEVER forget the "Bottom Riser Drop": you must saw off the thickness of ONE finished tread (e.g., 1 inch or 1.5 inches) from the VERY BOTTOM of your stringers! If you forget to drop the bottom of the stringer, Adding treads on top makes the first bottom step 1.5" too tall and the top step 1.5" too short—guaranteeing a failed building inspection and a tripping hazard.
Respect the 3/8-inch variance rule (IRC R311.7.5.1): the greatest riser height within any flight of stairs cannot exceed the smallest riser height by more than 3/8 inch.
Check Minimum Headroom (IRC R311.7.2): you must maintain at least 6 feet 8 inches (80 inches) of vertical headroom measured plumb from the outer nosing line of every tread up to the ceiling opening.
Clamp brass stair gauges (buttons) onto a framing square at your exact Riser and Tread marks so every step layout is identical.
Stop your circular saw cuts at the inside corner lines and finish the last 1.5 inches with a handsaw or jigsaw: over-cutting past the notch line weakens the remaining "throat" of the 2×12 stringer.
Maintain at least 5 inches of uncut wood ("effective throat depth") beneath the notches on 2×12 stringers.

faqs.question: What is the IRC building code for stair riser height and tread depth?
faqs.answer: Under the International Residential Code (IRC Section R311.7.5), the maximum riser height is 7-3/4 inches (7.75"), the minimum riser height is 4 inches, and the minimum tread depth is 10 inches measured horizontally from nosing to nosing. If tread depth is less than 11 inches, a nosing projection of 3/4" to 1-1/4" is required.

faqs.question: Why is the number of treads 1 less than the number of risers?
faqs.answer: On standard "dropped" or flush-mounted stringers (where the top of the stringer mounts one riser below the upper floor or deck rim joist), the upper landing itself serves as the final top step. Thus, 14 vertical climbs (risers) require only 13 horizontal steps (treads) on the stringer.

faqs.question: How many stair stringers do I need for a 36-inch or 48-inch staircase?
faqs.answer: Never use just 2 stringers! For a 36-inch-wide wood staircase, use 3 stringers (spaced 16 to 18 inches on-center). For a 48-inch-wide staircase or any stair using composite treads, use 4 stringers (spaced 12 to 16 inches on-center) so treads never flex.

faqs.question: What is the 7-11 rule for comfortable stairs?
faqs.answer: Architects use the "Rule of 17 to 18" (Rise + Run ≈ 17.5 to 18 inches), with a 7-inch riser and an 11-inch tread (7 + 11 = 18) considered the gold standard for natural human stride comfort and safety.

faqs.question: How do I convert decimal inches (like 7.71") to tape measure sixteenths?
faqs.answer: Multiply the decimal portion by 16 and round to the nearest whole sixteenth. For example, 0.71 × 16 = 11.36 sixteenths → 11/16 inch. So 7.71 inches equals 7-11/16 inches on your framing square.

inputs.name: pricePerSqFt

howToCalculate.formula: Rectangle = L × W; Triangle = 0.5 × B × H; Circle = π × (D ÷ 2)²; Trapezoid = ((B1 + B2) ÷ 2) × H; Sq Yards = Sq Ft ÷ 9
steps: Measure each side in feet and inches, then convert inches to decimal feet by dividing the inches by 12 (for example, 6 inches = 0.50 ft).
For a rectangle, multiply Length × Width.
For an L-shape or complex floor plan, divide the shape into two non-overlapping rectangles and add (L1 × W1) + (L2 × W2).
For a circle, divide the Diameter by 2 to get the Radius, square the radius (r × r), and multiply by 3.1416 (π).
Divide Square Feet by 9 for Square Yards, or multiply by 0.0929 for Square Meters.

workedExample.title: Calculating Square Footage of a 15 ft 6 in × 20 ft 3 in Room
workedExample.scenario: You measured a living room at 20 feet 3 inches long by 15 feet 6 inches wide.
steps: Convert inches to decimal feet: 3 in ÷ 12 = 0.25 ft (Length = 20.25 ft); 6 in ÷ 12 = 0.50 ft (Width = 15.50 ft).
Multiply Length × Width: 20.25 ft × 15.50 ft = 313.88 sq ft.
Convert to Square Yards: 313.88 ÷ 9 = 34.88 sq yd.
Add 10% material waste: 313.88 × 1.10 = 345.26 sq ft.
workedExample.finalAnswer: Net area is 313.88 sq ft (34.88 sq yd), or 345.26 sq ft with 10% material waste.

tipsAndMistakes: Never enter inches directly after a decimal point! 10 feet 6 inches is 10.50 feet (not 10.6 feet), and 10 feet 9 inches is 10.75 feet (not 10.9 feet). Use our built-in Feet + Inches inputs to avoid decimal errors.
To convert Square Inches to Square Feet, divide by 144 (never by 12!), because 12 in × 12 in = 144 sq in per square foot.
To convert Square Feet to Square Yards, divide by 9 (never by 3!), because 3 ft × 3 ft = 9 sq ft per square yard.
Break odd-shaped yards or rooms into simple rectangles and triangles on graph paper rather than guessing an average width.
For wall square footage, measure horizontal perimeter × ceiling height—don’t use floor square footage to buy paint or drywall.
Always add 5% to 15% waste when converting net square footage into building material orders.

faqs.question: How do I calculate square footage from inches?
faqs.answer: Either convert your inch measurements to feet first by dividing each side by 12 and then multiplying Length (ft) × Width (ft), OR multiply Length (in) × Width (in) to get square inches and divide the result by 144.

faqs.question: How many square feet are in an acre?
faqs.answer: One acre equals exactly 43,560 square feet (or 4,840 square yards). A quarter-acre suburban lot is 10,890 square feet—roughly 100 ft × 109 ft.

faqs.question: How do you find the square footage of a triangle or roof gable?
faqs.answer: Measure the horizontal base width in feet and multiply it by the vertical peak height in feet, then divide by 2 (Area = 0.5 × Base × Height). This works for both right triangles and symmetrical roof gables.

faqs.question: How do you calculate the square footage of a round patio or pool?
faqs.answer: Measure the full distance across the center of the circle (Diameter) and divide by 2 to get the Radius. Multiply Radius × Radius × 3.1416. For example, a 16-foot round patio has an 8-foot radius: 8 × 8 × 3.1416 = 201.06 square feet.

faqs.question: How do I convert square meters to square feet?
faqs.answer: Multiply square meters by 10.7639 to get square feet. Conversely, multiply square feet by 0.092903 to get square meters.

quickReferenceMeta.title: Cubic Feet, Cubic Yards & Tons for Common Areas & Depths

howToCalculate.formula: Cubic Feet = Area (sq ft) × (Depth_in ÷ 12); Cubic Yards = Cubic Feet ÷ 27
steps: Find your surface area in square feet (for a rectangle, multiply Length in feet × Width in feet).
Convert your Depth from inches to feet by dividing by 12 (e.g., 4 inches ÷ 12 = 0.333 feet).
Multiply Area (sq ft) × Depth (ft) to get volume in Cubic Feet.
Divide Cubic Feet by 27 (since a 3 ft × 3 ft × 3 ft cube = 27 cu ft) to convert into Cubic Yards.

workedExample.title: Calculating Cubic Yards for a 10×20 ft Area at 4 Inches Deep
workedExample.scenario: You are filling a 20 ft × 10 ft area to a depth of 4 inches with gravel (plus 5% settling).
steps: Surface Area = 20 ft × 10 ft = 200 sq ft.
Depth in Feet = 4 inches ÷ 12 = 0.3333 ft.
Net Cubic Feet = 200 × 0.3333 = 66.67 cu ft.
Net Cubic Yards = 66.67 ÷ 27 = 2.47 cu yd.
workedExample.finalAnswer: You need 2.59 cubic yards (70.0 cubic feet), which weighs ~3.63 tons of gravel.

tipsAndMistakes: Always divide Cubic Feet by 27 (never by 3 or 9!) to get Cubic Yards: a cubic yard is a cube measuring 3 feet long × 3 feet wide × 3 feet tall (3 × 3 × 3 = 27 cubic feet).
Watch your units: multiplying Length (in feet) × Width (in feet) × Depth (in inches) without dividing the inches by 12 first will overestimate your order by 1,200%!
Memorize the "324 Rule": 324 divided by your depth in inches tells you exactly how many square feet 1 cubic yard covers (324 ÷ 3" = 108 sq ft; 324 ÷ 4" = 81 sq ft; 324 ÷ 6" = 54 sq ft).
When excavating dirt for a patio or pool, remember the "Soil Swell Factor": 1 cubic yard of compacted dirt in the ground fluffs up to ~1.25 cubic yards of loose dirt in a dumpster!
Conversely, when buying loose gravel or topsoil to tamp down, add 10% extra for compaction shrinkage.
Check how your supplier prices materials: mulch, topsoil, and concrete are sold by the Cubic Yard, while quarry stone and sand are usually sold on a truck scale by the Ton.

faqs.question: How many cubic feet are in a cubic yard?
faqs.answer: There are exactly 27 cubic feet in 1 cubic yard (3 ft × 3 ft × 3 ft = 27 cu ft). Half a cubic yard is 13.5 cubic feet.

faqs.question: How much area does 1 cubic yard cover at 2, 3, 4, or 6 inches deep?
faqs.answer: One cubic yard (27 cu ft) covers 162 square feet at 2 inches deep, 108 square feet at 3 inches deep, 81 square feet at 4 inches deep, and 54 square feet at 6 inches deep.

faqs.question: How many wheelbarrows are in 1 cubic yard?
faqs.answer: A standard residential 6-cubic-foot wheelbarrow comfortably holds about 3 to 4 cubic feet of heavy dirt, gravel, or wet concrete per trip without spilling—meaning 1 cubic yard equals roughly 7 to 9 wheelbarrow loads.

faqs.question: How much does 1 cubic yard fit in a pickup truck bed?
faqs.answer: Volume-wise, a standard 6.5-foot pickup bed holds ~2 cubic yards heaped. However, WEIGHT is the real limit: 1 cubic yard of gravel (2,800 lbs) or topsoil (2,200 lbs) exceeds the 1,500-lb payload rating of most half-ton (F-150 / Silverado 1500) trucks! Only carry 1 full yard of heavy stone in a 3/4-ton (2500) or 1-ton truck.

faqs.question: How do I convert cubic yards to cubic meters?
faqs.answer: Multiply cubic yards by 0.764555 to get cubic meters (1 cubic yard ≈ 0.765 m³). Conversely, 1 cubic meter equals 1.308 cubic yards.

steps: Use the NOMINAL (rough-sawn) thickness in inches (1" for 4/4, 1.25" for 5/4, 2" for 8/4 or 2× lumber).

workedExample.title: Calculating Board Feet for Ten 2×6 × 12-Ft Boards
workedExample.scenario: You are buying 10 boards of nominal 2" × 6" × 12 ft lumber priced at $6.50 per board foot.
steps: Single Board (using inches) = (2 in × 6 in × 144 in) ÷ 144 = 12.0 board feet.

tipsAndMistakes: Always calculate board feet using NOMINAL rough dimensions, NOT actual surfaced dimensions! Even though a surfaced S4S 2×4 measures 1.5" × 3.5", lumberyards charge for the 2" × 4" rough log volume before planing.

Understand the "Quarter" system at hardwood dealers: thickness is written in quarters of an inch—4/4 ("four-quarter") = 1 inch rough (planes down to 13/16" or 3/4"); 5/4 = 1.25"; 6/4 = 1.5"; 8/4 = 2.0".
Note the thin-board rule: boards thinner than 1 inch (such as 3/4" or 1/2" surfaced boards) are still tallied as a full 1 inch thick when calculating board feet.
Add 20% to 30% waste when buying random-width, random-length (RWRL) rough hardwood: sapwood edges, end checks, knots, and jointer/planer kerfs eat up nearly a quarter of rough volume.
Bring a tape measure to the hardwood rack: random-width boards are tallied by rounding width to the nearest whole inch at the midpoint of the board.
Store rough hardwood stickers flat inside your heated workshop for at least 1 to 2 weeks before jointing and planing so internal stress equalizes.

faqs.question: What is 1 board foot of lumber?
faqs.answer: One board foot (1 BF or bd ft) is a volume measurement equal to a board that is 1 inch thick, 12 inches wide, and 12 inches (1 foot) long—which equals 144 cubic inches (or 1/12th of a cubic foot).

faqs.question: What is the difference between board feet and linear feet?
faqs.answer: Linear feet (LF) only measures length—ignoring how thick or wide the board is (used for trim and moulding of a fixed profile). Board feet (BF) measures three-dimensional wood volume (Thickness × Width × Length), so a 12-inch-wide board has twice as many board feet as a 6-inch-wide board of the same length.

faqs.question: How many board feet are in a standard 2×4 × 8-ft stud?
faqs.answer: Using nominal dimensions: (2 inches thick × 4 inches wide × 8 feet long) ÷ 12 = 5.33 board feet per 8-foot 2×4 stud.

faqs.question: What do S2S, S3S, and S4S mean when buying hardwood?
faqs.answer: Rough-sawn lumber comes straight off the sawmill blade. S2S means "Surfaced Two Sides" (planed flat on top and bottom to uniform thickness, with rough bark edges). S3S adds one straight-line ripped edge for your table saw fence, and S4S means "Surfaced Four Sides" (planed smooth on both faces and both edges).

faqs.question: How many board feet are in 1 cubic foot of wood?
faqs.answer: There are exactly 12 board feet in 1 cubic foot of lumber (since 1,728 cubic inches ÷ 144 cubic inches per board foot = 12).
